Cooling of the summit lava dome, which swells as it hardens
Tectonic subsidence that is unrelated to the volcano itself
Inflation, as magma recharges the system beneath the volcano
rationales: Deflation would make the ground sink and move inward.
Cooling rock contracts; it does not inflate the whole edifice.
The ground is rising, not subsiding, and the pattern centres on the volcano.
Correct. Ground rising and spreading outward records inflation, suggesting magma recharge.
questions.takeaway: Volcano inflation measured by GPS or InSAR suggests magma recharge.

questions.stem: Which of these is a deformation-monitoring method?
options: Tiltmeters and GPS measuring changes in the shape of the ground
Seismometers recording tremor from magma moving at depth
Thermal imaging to map new hot areas and growing lava domes
Gas sampling at fumaroles to track changes in volcanic emissions
rationales: Correct. Tiltmeters, GPS and surveying measure deformation, the changing shape of the volcano.
Seismometers monitor ground vibration, not deformation.
Thermal imaging is heat monitoring.
Gas sampling is gas monitoring.
questions.takeaway: Deformation monitoring uses tiltmeters, GPS, surveying and InSAR.

questions.stem: Which method uses the erupted material itself to estimate how deep the magma was stored?
options: Seismic tomography, mapping zones of slow waves
Infrasound, timing sound waves from the explosions
Petrology, analysing the chemistry of erupted rock
InSAR, comparing radar passes from before and after
rationales: Tomography images magma using seismic waves, not erupted rock.
Infrasound records explosions, not storage depth from rock chemistry.
Correct. Petrology uses geochemical analysis of erupted materials to estimate magma storage depth.
InSAR maps surface displacement, not rock chemistry.
questions.takeaway: Petrology reads magma storage depth from the chemistry of erupted rock.

questions.stem: Which statement describes the grand challenge of volcanology given in the notes?
options: To forecast the onset, size, duration and hazard of eruptions
To predict the exact minute of each eruption years in advance
To map every past eruption of every volcano since it formed
To prevent eruptions by draining magma from volcanic chambers
rationales: Correct. The grand challenge is improving our ability to forecast the onset, size, duration and hazard of eruptions.
Forecasting aims at onset, size, duration and hazard, not exact timing years ahead.
Past records help, but the stated challenge is forecasting future eruptions.
The goal is forecasting, not preventing eruptions.
questions.takeaway: Volcanology's grand challenge: forecast onset, size, duration and hazard of eruptions.

questions.stem: Authorities close a volcano based on deformation and tremor, but a landslide unexpectedly exposes the magma and triggers a sideways blast that kills people outside the main exclusion zone. What lesson does this teach?
options: Closing a volcano to the public never reduces the number of deaths
Hazard zones must allow for unexpected styles like lateral blasts
Deformation and tremor are not useful signs that an eruption is coming
Eruptions always go straight up, so hazard maps never need changing
rationales: Closure reduced exposure; the deaths came from an unexpected eruption style.
Correct. Monitoring correctly flagged the danger, but the lateral blast was a style the zones did not anticipate. Hazard maps were redrawn afterwards.
Deformation and tremor were what led authorities to close the volcano.
The blast went sideways, which is exactly why hazard maps had to change.
questions.takeaway: Hazard zoning must allow for eruption styles that monitoring may not anticipate.

questions.stem: A very large eruption kills far fewer people than it might have. Which combination of measures from the notes best explains this?
options: Holding all warnings back until the eruption had clearly started
Stronger roofs built in the towns nearest to the volcano's main vent
Draining the crater lake in advance so that no lahars could form
Defined evacuation zones, staged alert levels and daily alerts
rationales: Warnings worked because they came before the major eruption.
Most of the deaths that did happen were from roof collapse, so roofs were not what saved lives.
This is not a measure the notes describe.
Correct. Scientists worked with local authorities to set evacuation zones and alert stages, announced daily, so tens of thousands were evacuated beforehand.
questions.takeaway: Evacuation zones, staged alerts and clear communication save lives.

questions.stem: In a four-level volcano alert system running Normal, Caution, Watch, Warning, what does a move from Caution up to Watch signal?
options: Heightened unrest, with a strong potential to erupt
Minor unrest only, just slightly above the baseline
A return to baseline activity with no eruption threat
An eruption that is imminent or already under way
rationales: Correct. Watch (Level III) means heightened unrest with a strong potential for eruption.
That is Level II, Caution, the level being left behind.
That is Level I, Normal.
That is Level IV, Warning.
questions.takeaway: Alert levels: Normal → Caution (minor unrest) → Watch (strong potential) → Warning (imminent or ongoing).

questions.stem: On a volcanic hazard zone map, which zone should be evacuated first when the alert level begins to rise?
options: Every zone at once, since the zone boundaries ignore the hazard type
Any zone downwind, because ash fall is the deadliest volcanic hazard
The zone nearest the vent, exposed to pyroclastic flows and lava
The outermost zone, exposed only to rain lahars and light ash fall
rationales: Zones are drawn by hazard type and severity, so evacuation is staged.
Ash fall is widespread, but pyroclastic flows near the vent are the more deadly threat.
Correct. The innermost zone faces extreme risk from pyroclastic flows, lava flows and lahars and is evacuated immediately when alert levels rise.
The outer zone faces the lowest risk and is evacuated last.
questions.takeaway: Hazard zones stage evacuation: the zone nearest the vent goes first.

questions.stem: Under what condition does a slope fail?
options: When the frictional resistance exceeds the driving force
When the driving force exceeds the frictional resistance
When the driving force and the resistance become equal
When the load on the slope falls below a set threshold
rationales: If resistance exceeds the driving force, the material stays in place.
Correct. A landslide happens when the driving force (F) is greater than the frictional resistance (f).
Balanced forces mean the slope is on the edge of failure but not yet moving.
Reducing load lowers the driving force, which makes failure less likely.
questions.takeaway: Slope failure: F (driving force) > f (frictional resistance).

questions.stem: A slope is made steeper while the material on it stays the same. What happens to the forces?
options: Driving force falls and frictional resistance rises, so failure becomes less likely
Driving force rises, but resistance rises faster, so the slope becomes safer
Both forces rise by the same amount, so the slope's stability does not change
Driving force rises and frictional resistance falls, so failure becomes likelier
rationales: This reverses both effects.
Frictional resistance falls with steepening, because the force normal to the slope falls.
The two forces move in opposite directions as the slope steepens.
Correct. As slope angle increases, sin(angle) rises so the force parallel to the slope rises, while cos(angle) falls so the normal force and friction fall.
questions.takeaway: Steeper slope: more driving force, less friction, so more likely to slide.

questions.stem: Two identical blocks rest on two slopes, one gentle and one steep. Which experiences the larger driving force, and why?
options: Neither, as both blocks have the same load and so the same driving force
The gentle one, as a longer slope gives gravity more distance to act on
The steep one, as driving force scales with the sine of the slope angle
The steep one, as steeper slopes add extra cohesion to the material
rationales: Same load, but the share acting along the slope depends on the angle.
Slope length does not enter the driving force; the angle does.
Correct. Driving force = load × sin(slope angle), so the steeper slope gives a larger force parallel to the slope.
Cohesion is part of resistance, not driving force, and steepness does not add it.
questions.takeaway: Driving force = load × sin(slope angle).

questions.stem: A river is eroding the base of a hillside while new houses are being built along its top. Why does this combination raise landslide risk?
options: Both add cohesion, but this is outweighed by the rising river level
Both remove load, so the friction holding the slope in place drops
Both lower the slope angle, so material piles up and later collapses
Both steepen or load the slope, increasing the driving force on it
rationales: Neither adds cohesion; both act on the driving force.
Building on top adds load rather than removing it.
Undercutting the base steepens the slope rather than flattening it.
Correct. Undercutting by streams steepens the slope and removes support, and construction loads the upper slope. Both increase the driving force.
questions.takeaway: Undercutting the base and loading the top both raise the driving force.

questions.stem: Which factor adds to a slope's driving force only some of the time, rather than acting constantly?
options: Earthquake shaking adding a dynamic force
The load or weight of the slope material
The cohesion holding the soil grains together
The slope angle set by the landscape
rationales: Correct. External forces such as earthquake shaking add dynamic forcing to the driving force, but they are not always present.
Load is a constant base factor in the driving force.
Cohesion is part of the resisting force, not the driving force.
Slope angle is a constant base factor in the driving force.
questions.takeaway: Slope angle and load are base driving factors; shaking is an extra, occasional one.

questions.stem: What is the angle of repose?
options: The angle at which a rotational slide's head tilts back
The steepest angle at which loose material stays stable
The slope angle at which friction falls to exactly zero
The gentlest angle at which a landslide can still begin
rationales: Rotational slides rotate backward, but that is not the angle of repose.
Correct. The angle of repose is the steepest angle at which any loose material is stable.
Friction does not vanish at the angle of repose; the slope is just at its stable limit.
It is a maximum stable angle, not a minimum failure angle.
questions.takeaway: Angle of repose: the steepest stable angle for loose material.

questions.stem: Two piles of dry, loose material are built up until they start to slump. Which pile can hold the steeper angle of repose?
options: Any pile, since the angle depends only on its height
Any pile, since the angle depends only on gravity
Large, angular grains that lock into one another
Small, rounded grains that roll easily past each other
rationales: Height is not one of the controls; grain shape, size and moisture are.
Gravity is the same for both piles; grain properties make the difference.
Correct. The angle of repose depends on the angularity and size of the grains (and moisture). Angular grains interlock and can stand steeper.
Rounded grains roll past each other, so they settle at gentler angles.
questions.takeaway: Angle of repose depends on grain angularity, size and moisture.

questions.stem: After a forested hillside is cleared, landslides there become more frequent. What best explains this?
options: The trees were adding load that helped press the slope into place
Trees soak up all the rain, so without them slopes dry out
Clearing makes the slope steeper by removing the tree trunks
The roots that bound the soil had been providing resisting force
rationales: Added load increases the driving force; trees help mainly through their roots.
A drier slope would not explain more landslides; losing root strength does.
Removing trees does not change the slope angle.
Correct. Vegetation roots bind the soil and provide resisting force, so removing them reduces f.
questions.takeaway: Removing vegetation removes the resisting force that roots provide.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the planar internal weaknesses that the notes say slopes can fail along?
options: A uniform mass of homogeneous material
Contacts between rocks of different strength
Fractures or old landslide slip surfaces
Layers within a sedimentary rock
rationales: Correct. Homogeneous material has no planar weakness; it tends to fail on a curved surface as a rotational slide.
Contacts between rocks of different strength are listed weaknesses.
Fractures, faults and old slip surfaces are listed weaknesses.
Sedimentary layers are listed as planar weaknesses.
questions.takeaway: Planar weaknesses: bedding, fractures, faults, old slip surfaces, rock contacts. Homogeneous material lacks them.

questions.stem: Why does a sandcastle keep its shape best with a little water, rather than when dry or soaked?
options: Dry sand has the most cohesion, and a little water adds load to hold it
A little water adds cohesion through surface tension between the grains
Water raises the pore pressure, pushing the grains more tightly together
Soaked sand has the most friction, so the shape fails only as it dries
rationales: Dry sand has little cohesion; that is why it slumps.
Correct. Cohesion comes from the surface tension of water between loose grains. A slight amount of water helps, but too little or too much does not.
Higher pore pressure reduces friction and pushes grains apart.
Saturated sand loses strength as pore pressure rises.
questions.takeaway: A little water adds cohesion; too much raises pore pressure and weakens the slope.

questions.stem: After days of heavy rain, the groundwater level inside a slope rises. Why might the slope now fail?
options: The water dissolves the slope rock, removing material from the base
Rising pore fluid pressure reduces the friction between the grains
The water lowers the slope's load, so the driving force disappears
The rain adds cohesion, which drags the grains downslope together
rationales: The mechanism in the notes is pore pressure reducing friction, not dissolution.
Correct. Increased pore fluid pressure reduces friction and makes landslides easier.
Water adds weight, so it does not remove the driving force.
Cohesion holds grains together; it does not pull them downslope.
questions.takeaway: Higher pore fluid pressure reduces friction and promotes landslides.

questions.stem: Which statement about water in a slope is most accurate?
options: Water always stabilises a slope, because it binds the grains together
Water has no effect on friction, only on the angle of the slope
A little adds cohesion, but a lot adds load and raises pore pressure
Water always destabilises a slope, because it only ever adds weight
rationales: Too much water weakens a slope by raising pore pressure.
Water affects friction through pore pressure and cohesion.
Correct. Slight moisture adds cohesion, but more water adds weight (load) and raises pore pressure, reducing friction.
Some water helps, through cohesion.
questions.takeaway: Water cuts both ways: a little adds cohesion, a lot adds load and pore pressure.

questions.stem: What happens during soil liquefaction?
options: Dry soil becomes so cohesive that it cracks apart into hard blocks
Heavy rain slowly dissolves the soil grains into a thick, sticky mud
Heat from below melts the soil until it begins to flow like lava
Rapid shaking makes wet soil lose stiffness and act like a fluid
rationales: Liquefaction involves loss of strength in wet soil, not dry soil cracking.
Liquefaction is caused by shaking, not by rain dissolving grains.
No melting is involved.
Correct. Liquefaction occurs when rapid ground shaking causes soils to lose stiffness and behave like a viscous fluid.
questions.takeaway: Liquefaction: shaking makes saturated soil lose stiffness and behave like a fluid.

questions.stem: Where are the effects of liquefaction during earthquakes usually most severe?
options: Coasts and river deltas with young, saturated deposits
Mountain ridges built of old, dry and unbroken bedrock
Steep slopes of dry rock far away from rivers or coasts
Desert plains where the soil has dried out completely
rationales: Correct. Liquefaction is especially severe in coastal areas and river deltas, where young, saturated deposits are common.
Old, dry bedrock does not liquefy.
Dry rock does not liquefy.
Liquefaction needs saturated soil.
questions.takeaway: Liquefaction hits young, saturated deposits in coasts and deltas hardest.

questions.stem: After an earthquake, a large building on pile foundations is left tilted but structurally largely intact. What most likely caused this?
options: Liquefaction took away the soil support around its piles
Resonance made the building sway until it leaned to one side
A rockfall struck one side and toppled the building sideways
Creep pushed the building over during the minutes of shaking
rationales: Correct. Structures on pile foundations can lose support from the adjacent soil during liquefaction and come to rest at a tilt.
Resonance damages the structure itself rather than tilting an intact building.
Nothing in the scenario points to a rockfall.
Creep is very slow and happens over years, not during shaking.
questions.takeaway: Liquefaction removes soil support, leaving intact buildings tilted.

questions.stem: Which matches each type of mass movement to its typical speed?
options: Rockfall: fast; debris flow: very fast; slide: slow; creep: moderate
Rockfall: very fast; debris flow: fast; slide: moderate; creep: slow
Rockfall: slow; debris flow: moderate; slide: very fast; creep: fast
Rockfall: moderate; debris flow: slow; slide: fast; creep: very fast
rationales: Rockfall is the fastest, and creep is the slowest.
Correct. Rockfall is very fast, debris flows are fast, rotational and translational slides are moderate, and creep is slow.
Rockfall is very fast and creep is slow.
This nearly reverses the order.
questions.takeaway: Speed: rockfall > debris flow > slides > creep.

questions.stem: Which type of mass movement typically has the longest runout?
options: A rockfall, which moves the fastest of all the types
Creep, which keeps moving steadily for many years
A debris flow, which can travel tens of kilometres
A rotational slide, moving along a curved surface
rationales: Rockfall is very fast but has a short runout.
Creep moves for years but only short distances.
Correct. Debris flows have long runouts and can travel tens of kilometres.
Rotational slides move short distances.
questions.takeaway: Debris flows travel furthest; rockfall is fastest but short.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes rotational slides from translational slides?
options: Both move on planar surfaces, but translational ones rotate backward
Both move on curved surfaces, but rotational slides move much faster
Rotational slides move on planar surfaces; translational on curved ones
Rotational slides move on curved surfaces; translational on planar ones
rationales: Rotational slides move on curved surfaces; it is their heads that rotate backward.
Translational slides move on planar surfaces and tend to be faster.
The surfaces are swapped.
Correct. Rotational slides move above a curved slip surface, with the head rotating backward; translational slides move on a planar surface.
questions.takeaway: Rotational = curved slip surface; translational = planar slip surface.

questions.stem: A hillside is built of rock layers that dip parallel to the slope, with a weak clay-rich layer between them. What type of failure is most likely?
options: Liquefaction, as clay layers turn to fluid easily
A translational slide along the planar clay layer
Creep only, as layered rock cannot fail suddenly
A rotational slide on a deep, curved slip surface
rationales: Liquefaction affects saturated sandy deposits during shaking, not a buried clay plane.
Correct. Translational slides move on planar slip surfaces such as joints, faults or clay-rich layers.
Layered rock with a weak plane can fail quickly as a translational slide.
Rotational slides favour homogeneous material without planar weaknesses.
questions.takeaway: A planar weakness parallel to the slope favours translational sliding.

questions.stem: For rotational and translational slides of similar size, which tends to travel faster and further, and why?
options: Neither, as speed depends only on the volume of material, not its path
Rotational, as its curved surface acts like a ramp that launches the whole mass
Rotational, as its backward-rotating head pushes the toe far out ahead
Translational, as it keeps sliding while its planar surface slopes down
rationales: The notes link travel distance to slide type and slip surface, not volume alone.
Rotational slides move short distances; the curved surface does not launch them.
The toe of a rotational slide moves up onto the landscape, which limits its travel.
Correct. Translational slides often move faster and farther, continuing as long as they are on a downward-inclined surface and a driving mass exists.
questions.takeaway: Translational slides tend to go faster and further than rotational ones.

questions.stem: Fences and walls on a hillside slowly tilt and crack over several years, with no sudden event. What is happening?
options: Creep, slowly moving the ground and damaging brittle structures
Rockfall, dropping debris onto the structures from cliffs above
A debris flow, burying the structures beneath wet sediment
Liquefaction, as shaking turns the soil beneath them to fluid
rationales: Correct. Creep is slow, with short runout, and damages brittle structures through gradual ground movement.
Rockfall is sudden and very fast.
Debris flows are fast and bury what they hit.
Liquefaction happens during shaking, not gradually over years.
questions.takeaway: Creep: slow ground movement that gradually damages brittle structures.

questions.stem: Which factors most control how damaging a debris flow is?
options: The time of day and the season in which the flow happens
The cohesion of the source slope before it began to fail
Sediment concentration, debris content, velocity and depth
Slope angle at the source only, whatever the flow contains
rationales: Timing may affect exposure, but the notes link impact to the flow's properties.
Cohesion affects whether the slope fails, not how damaging the resulting flow is.
Correct. The level of debris-flow impact relates to sediment concentration, debris content, velocity and depth.
Source slope matters for triggering, but impact depends on the flow itself.
questions.takeaway: Debris-flow impact scales with sediment concentration, debris content, velocity and depth.

questions.stem: A slope is overloaded at its top. Which engineering measure adds resistance to sliding?
options: Cutting into the slope base to make room
Clearing vegetation from the whole slope
Adding load to the lower part of the slope
Adding more load to the upper part of the slope
rationales: Cutting the base undercuts the slope and makes it less stable.
Removing roots reduces resisting force.
Correct. Weighting the bottom adds mass at the lower part of the slope, increasing the resisting force.
More load at the top increases the driving force.
questions.takeaway: Weight the bottom, not the top, to stabilise a slope.

questions.stem: Engineers install drainage pipes inside a slope. Which part of the force balance does this mainly target?
options: It lowers the slope angle, which cuts the driving force directly
It lowers pore pressure, restoring friction that resists sliding
It removes the load of the soil by washing the soil away
It adds cohesion by drying the whole slope out completely
rationales: Drainage does not change the slope's geometry.
Correct. Draining water lowers pore fluid pressure, which restores friction and resistance.
Drainage removes water, not the soil itself.
Completely dry soil loses the cohesion that slight moisture gives.
questions.takeaway: Drainage works by lowering pore pressure and restoring friction.

questions.stem: What is cable mesh draped over a rock cliff mainly designed to reduce?
options: Liquefaction of the soil during earthquakes
Pore pressure building up inside the slope
Creep slowly deforming the slope over years
Rockfall reaching the roads and homes below
rationales: Liquefaction affects saturated soil, not rock faces.
Pore pressure is managed with drainage, not mesh.
Mesh holds loose rock at the surface; it does not stop slow creep.
Correct. Cable mesh is used to reduce rockfall risk.
questions.takeaway: Cable mesh is a rockfall mitigation measure.

questions.stem: Which pairing of landslide monitoring approach with example is correct?
options: In-situ: instruments placed on site; remote: LiDAR and optical imagery
In-situ: statistical rainfall models; remote: field mapping on foot
In-situ: LiDAR and optical imagery; remote: instruments placed on site
In-situ: satellite radar imaging; remote: sensors buried in the slope
rationales: Correct. In situ means on site, so in-situ monitoring uses instruments placed on the slope. LiDAR and optical imagery observe from afar.
Statistical models are not in-situ instruments, and field mapping is done on site.
The two are swapped.
Satellite imaging is remote, and buried sensors are in situ.
questions.takeaway: In situ = on site; remote = imagery such as LiDAR and optical.

questions.stem: A hilly city wants to estimate how many landslides a major rainstorm might trigger across its whole territory. Which approach from the notes fits?
options: A single in-situ sensor placed in the city's steepest slope
Seismic tomography mapping slow-wave zones beneath the hills
A statistical index linking rainstorms to landslide numbers
Infrasound stations listening for slopes as they begin to fail
rationales: One sensor monitors one slope, not landslide numbers across a territory.
Tomography images magma beneath volcanoes, not landslide potential.
Correct. A Landslide Potential Index is a statistical model used to estimate the potential number of landslides triggered across a territory during a major rainstorm.
Infrasound is a volcano-monitoring method in the notes.
questions.takeaway: Statistical indices link rainstorms to expected landslide numbers across a region.

questions.stem: Imagery of a hillside shows many landslide scars of different ages. What does this most suggest about the hillside?
options: It has used up all its loose material and is now likely to be stable
The scars all came from one event, which has since ended the hazard
The scars mark slopes protected by mitigation, so the risk is now low
It has failed repeatedly, so future landslides there are likely
rationales: Repeated failure suggests ongoing instability, not exhaustion.
Different ages mean different events over time.
Scars mark past failures, not mitigation.
Correct. Scars from landslides at different times show repeated failure, which points to continuing hazard.
questions.takeaway: Landslide scars of many ages signal a slope that keeps failing.

questions.stem: Monitoring shows a mountainside becoming unstable, and a village below is evacuated. A week later a huge rock-ice avalanche destroys most of the village. What does this show?
options: The loss of property proves the monitoring system had failed entirely
Monitoring can save lives by prompting evacuation, even when property is lost
Monitoring can stop an avalanche, provided it detects the instability early
Evacuation is only worthwhile when the expected avalanche is a small one
rationales: The monitoring did its job: people were moved before the event.
Correct. Almost all residents had been evacuated after authorities grew concerned about the mountain's stability, so monitoring protected lives even though the village was destroyed.
Monitoring warns; it cannot stop the slope failing.
Evacuation matters most when the event is large.
questions.takeaway: Monitoring and evacuation protect lives even when property cannot be saved.

questions.stem: When does a cascade of hazards occur?
options: When one hazardous event triggers or raises the likelihood of another
When two unrelated hazards happen to strike the same place by chance
When a single hazard grows steadily larger over a long period of time
When one hazard affects several different countries at the same time
rationales: Correct. When one hazardous event triggers or increases the likelihood of another, it creates a cascade of hazards.
A cascade needs a causal link, not coincidence.
Growth of one hazard is not a cascade of hazards.
That describes a transboundary hazard, not a cascade.
questions.takeaway: Cascade: one hazard triggers or raises the likelihood of another.

questions.stem: A wildfire burns a steep watershed. The following winter brings heavy rain. Which hazard becomes much more likely, and why?
options: Liquefaction, as burned soil becomes saturated and loses all its stiffness
Debris flows, as burned soil repels water and runoff carries sediment away
Creep, as the loss of trees lets the slope deform slowly over many years
Rockfall, as heat from the fire cracks the bedrock into loose falling blocks
rationales: Liquefaction needs earthquake shaking of saturated deposits, not rainfall on burned slopes.
Correct. Fire can leave a water-repellent soil layer, so rain runs off and picks up loose sediment, feeding debris flows.
Creep is slow, while the fire-then-rain cascade produces fast flows.
The notes link fire and rain to debris flows, not rockfall.
questions.takeaway: Fire then heavy rain is a classic cascade into debris flows.

questions.stem: After an earthquake, a landslide blocks a river valley. Why is this dangerous for towns far downstream?
options: The dam raises groundwater, causing liquefaction in towns far downstream
The dam triggers aftershocks as the water piling up presses on the fault
The dam stops the river, so towns downstream lose their flood risk entirely
The landslide dam can burst suddenly, sending a flood far down the valley
rationales: This is not the mechanism; the threat is a sudden outburst flood.
The danger is the dam failing, not triggered aftershocks.
Blocking the river creates a growing lake behind the dam, adding risk.
Correct. Landslides can dam rivers. When such a dam bursts, the outburst flood can travel very far downstream.
questions.takeaway: Earthquake → landslide dam → outburst flood is a key cascade.

questions.stem: A large river flood is followed weeks later by broken submarine cables far offshore. Which cascade links the two?
options: The flood fed a turbidity current that raced down a submarine canyon
The flood raised sea level, lifting the cables until they snapped
The flood triggered an earthquake that broke the cables on the seafloor
The flood warmed the sea, making the cables expand until they broke
rationales: Correct. Turbidity currents are submarine debris flows; a river flood can trigger one that travels far along the seafloor, breaking cables in its path.
Floods do not lift cables off the seafloor.
No earthquake is needed to explain this cascade.
This is not a mechanism in the notes.
questions.takeaway: Turbidity currents (submarine debris flows) can be triggered by floods and break seafloor cables.

questions.stem: Why do large earthquakes in steep, mountainous terrain often trigger thousands of landslides?
options: Shaking lowers slope angles, so material piles up and then collapses
Shaking increases friction, so slopes lock in place and later fail at once
Shaking adds dynamic force, raising the driving force on unstable slopes
Shaking removes load from the slopes, so the resisting force drops away
rationales: Shaking does not reduce slope angles in this way.
Shaking reduces resistance rather than locking slopes.
Correct. Ground shaking adds dynamic forcing that increases the driving force and can dislodge large masses of unstable rock and soil.
Shaking does not remove load; it adds dynamic force.
questions.takeaway: Earthquake shaking adds dynamic driving force, triggering widespread landslides.

questions.stem: A reservoir is filled behind a new dam in a valley with unstable slopes. Which cascade is the main concern?
options: The dam's weight sets off a volcanic eruption that drains the whole reservoir
The lake lowers nearby groundwater, drying the slopes until they crumble away
The reservoir cools the valley, freezing the slopes into solid, stable blocks
Water soaks the slopes, a slide falls into the lake, a wave overtops the dam
rationales: Dams do not trigger eruptions in the notes.
Filling a reservoir raises nearby water levels rather than lowering them.
This is not a mechanism in the notes.
Correct. Raising a reservoir can increase landslide risk; a landslide into the lake displaces water into a wave that can overtop the dam and destroy towns downstream.
questions.takeaway: Reservoirs can trigger landslides that displace water into destructive waves.

questions.stem: A strike-slip earthquake, a type that rarely makes large tsunamis, is followed by a damaging tsunami in a long, narrow bay. What best explains this?
options: Submarine landslides displaced water, and the narrow bay amplified it
The earthquake was deep, and deep events produce the largest tsunamis
Liquefaction on land pushed water out to sea, forming the tsunami wave
Strike-slip faults always uplift the seafloor, so a tsunami was expected
rationales: Correct. The tsunami came from submarine landslides (plus possible seafloor movement), and the narrow bay amplified the wave.
Shallow, not deep, events are linked with large tsunamis.
Liquefaction caused landslides on land, but the tsunami came from underwater slides.
Strike-slip motion is mainly horizontal and does not usually uplift the seafloor.
questions.takeaway: Submarine landslides can turn a strike-slip earthquake into a tsunami disaster.

questions.stem: According to the UNDRR view highlighted in the notes, which change would most directly stop a hurricane from becoming a disaster for a town?
options: Relying on natural processes, since disasters are purely natural events
Reducing the town's vulnerability and making sure it is protected
Forecasting the hurricane more precisely, with no other action taken
Reducing the hurricane's physical strength before it reaches the town
rationales: The point of the UNDRR campaign is that there are no natural disasters, only natural hazards.
Correct. A natural hazard only becomes a disaster when it impacts a community that is not adequately protected and whose population is vulnerable through poverty, exclusion or social disadvantage.
Forecasts alone do not reduce vulnerability or protection.
We cannot weaken a hurricane; the notes focus on protection and vulnerability.
questions.takeaway: There are no natural disasters: hazards become disasters through vulnerability and lack of protection.

questions.stem: Which of these statements describes climate rather than weather?
options: The record high temperature measured at the airport last week
The thunderstorm that flooded the town centre this afternoon
The region's usual rainy-season pattern over recent decades
The strong winds forecast for tomorrow along the eastern coast
rationales: One day's temperature, even a record, is weather; climate looks at the long-term pattern.
A single storm on a particular afternoon is weather: the state of the atmosphere at a place and time.
Correct. Climate is the long-term pattern of weather in a region, usually assessed over 30 years or more.
Tomorrow's winds at one coast are weather.
questions.takeaway: Weather = the atmosphere at a place and time; climate = the long-term pattern, over 30+ years.

questions.stem: After an unusually hot week, someone claims this proves the local climate has changed. What is wrong with the claim?
options: A week is too long, as climate describes conditions at a single moment
One week is weather; climate is the long-term pattern over decades
Climate is fixed by latitude alone, so it can never change over time
Climate refers to rainfall only, so changes in temperature don't count
rationales: This reverses the two: the state at a single time is weather, not climate.
Correct. A hot week is weather. Climate describes the long-term pattern, usually assessed over 30 years or more, so one week cannot show a change in climate.
Latitude strongly influences climate, but climate can still change over time.
Climate covers all aspects of weather, including temperature, rain and wind.
questions.takeaway: A short spell of unusual weather does not by itself show that the climate has changed.

questions.stem: Why do polar regions receive less solar energy per unit area than the equator?
options: Sunlight arrives at a shallow angle, spreading out and crossing more atmosphere
The poles receive fewer hours of daylight on every single day of the whole year
The poles are under cloud all year round, which reflects almost all incoming sunlight
The poles are further from the Sun, so the sunlight that reaches them is much weaker
rationales: Correct. Near the poles sunlight strikes at a shallow angle, so the same energy spreads over a larger area, and it travels further through the atmosphere, losing more to scattering and absorption.
Polar summers have very long days. The difference comes from the angle of sunlight and the longer path through the atmosphere.
Cloud cover is not the explanation the notes give.
The distance difference between latitudes is negligible; the angle of sunlight is what matters.
questions.takeaway: Shallow sun angle and a longer path through the atmosphere give the poles less energy per unit area.

questions.stem: A student argues that summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun at that time of year. Which observation best refutes this?
options: Seasons are just as strong at the equator as they are near the poles
Earth is closest to the Sun in July, during the northern summer
Earth's orbit is perfectly circular, so its distance never changes
The two hemispheres have their summers at opposite times of the year
rationales: Seasonal changes are stronger towards the poles and weaker near the equator.
Earth is actually a bit closer to the Sun in January, during the northern winter.
The orbit is not completely circular; there are small differences in distance through the year.
Correct. If distance caused summer, both hemispheres would have summer at the same time. The tilt of Earth's axis is the reason for seasons.
questions.takeaway: Seasons come from the tilt of Earth's axis, not distance from the Sun.

questions.stem: If Earth's axis had no tilt at all, what would happen to the seasons?
options: They would become much stronger, since the poles would face the Sun far more directly
They would stay as they are, since seasons come from Earth's distance to the Sun
They would largely disappear, as the zone of strongest heating would stop shifting
They would only happen at the equator, where the sunlight is the most direct
rationales: Without tilt, the poles would never face the Sun more directly; they would always get shallow sunlight.
Seasons come from the tilt, not distance.
Correct. Seasons happen because the tilt shifts the latitude receiving the most direct sunlight through the year. Without tilt, that shift would stop.
Seasonal changes are weakest near the equator, and without tilt they would largely vanish everywhere.
questions.takeaway: No tilt, no shifting zone of strongest heating, and so essentially no seasons.

questions.stem: Where on Earth are seasonal changes strongest?
options: Over the oceans, which store heat from one season to the next
Equally everywhere, since the whole planet is tilted
At the equator, where the midday Sun is often overhead
Towards the poles, where the tilt changes sunlight the most
rationales: The notes link seasonal strength to latitude, not to oceans.
The tilt affects latitudes differently, so seasons are not equal everywhere.
The equator receives fairly direct sunlight all year, so its seasons are weak.
Correct. Seasonal changes are stronger towards the poles and weaker near the equator.
questions.takeaway: Seasons strengthen towards the poles and weaken near the equator.

questions.stem: What is the weather and climate system fundamentally doing?
options: Moving excess heat from the poles towards the equator
Moving excess heat from the equator towards the poles
Holding heat where it lands, keeping latitudes separate
Moving heat out of the oceans down into the deep Earth
rationales: The equator has the surplus of energy, so heat moves away from it.
Correct. The system is a giant mechanism trying to redress the unequal distribution of energy, moving excess heat from the equator towards the poles, fastest through the atmosphere.
The system actively redistributes heat rather than holding it in place.
The redistribution happens through the atmosphere and oceans, not into the deep Earth.
questions.takeaway: Weather and climate redistribute heat from the equator towards the poles.

questions.stem: Why does a parcel of air cool as it rises?
options: It expands under lower pressure, and expanding uses energy
It loses heat to the colder air that surrounds it as it rises
It moves further and further away from the warm ground beneath it
It takes up moisture, which draws the heat out of it
rationales: Correct. Rising air expands because pressure is lower at height, and expansion takes energy, so the air cools without gaining or losing heat. This is adiabatic cooling.
Adiabatic cooling happens without heat being exchanged with the surroundings.
Distance from the ground is not the mechanism; expansion under lower pressure is.
Taking up moisture is not why rising air cools.
questions.takeaway: Rising air cools adiabatically: it expands under lower pressure.

questions.stem: Why does rising air cool more slowly once a cloud has formed in it?
options: Clouds block sunlight, so the air no longer needs to cool any further
Water droplets absorb the cold from the air, keeping the air warmer
Condensation releases latent heat, which offsets some of the cooling
Saturated air is denser, so it rises more slowly and expands less
rationales: Sunlight is not the reason the cooling rate changes.
Droplets release heat as they form; they do not absorb cold.
Correct. Before cloud forms the rate is about 10°C per kilometre; once cloud forms it averages about 5°C per kilometre, because condensation releases heat.
Humid air is actually less dense; the slower cooling comes from latent heat release.
questions.takeaway: Once cloud forms, latent heat from condensation slows the cooling of rising air.

questions.stem: Air rising from the surface cools until it reaches its dew point. What happens next?
options: The air expands faster, so its rate of cooling doubles
The air sinks and warms again back down to ground level
Water vapour condenses into tiny droplets, forming cloud
All moisture is removed, leaving the air completely dry
rationales: Once cloud forms, cooling actually slows because latent heat is released.
Reaching the dew point does not make the air sink.
Correct. At the dew point the air reaches 100% relative humidity and cannot hold more vapour, so it condenses into droplets and forms a cloud.
Condensation begins at the dew point; it does not instantly remove all moisture.
questions.takeaway: At the dew point, rising air saturates and cloud forms.

questions.stem: At the same temperature and pressure, how does humid air compare with dry air?
options: It is equally dense, as density depends on heat alone
It is less dense, as vapour displaces heavier gases
It is denser, as it carries extra molecules of water
It is denser, as liquid water is heavier than the air is
rationales: Density also depends on the type of gas molecules, not only on temperature.
Correct. Water vapour displaces some of the heavier nitrogen and oxygen, so humid air is less dense than dry air and rises faster.
Equal volumes of gas at the same temperature and pressure hold the same number of molecules, so vapour replaces heavier ones rather than adding extra.
Liquid water is denser than air, but water vapour is less dense than dry air.
questions.takeaway: Humid air is less dense than dry air, so it rises faster.

questions.stem: Moist air rises and its water vapour begins to condense. What happens to the upward motion?
options: Released latent heat warms the air, so it keeps rising in a feedback
The air stops rising at once, as the cloud acts as a lid on convection
Nothing changes, as condensation neither adds nor removes any heat
Condensation makes the air heavier, so it soon sinks to the surface
rationales: Correct. Condensation releases latent heat, warming the surrounding air so it expands and keeps rising: a feedback loop that moves heat upward.
Clouds do not cap the rising air; the heat released helps it rise further.
Condensation releases a large amount of latent heat.
The latent heat makes the air more buoyant, not heavier.
questions.takeaway: Latent heat from condensation feeds further rising: humid air moves heat upward efficiently.

questions.stem: Why does air that cools tend to produce cloud and rain?
options: Cooling makes air rise faster, flinging droplets up into clouds
Cooler air can hold more water vapour, so it draws in moisture
Cooling raises the air pressure, squeezing water out of the air
Cooler air can hold less water vapour, so the excess condenses
rationales: Cooling air tends to sink, not rise faster.
This reverses the relationship between temperature and water vapour.
The key factor is the drop in how much vapour the air can hold, not pressure squeezing it out.
Correct. Warm air can hold more water vapour than cold air. When air cools it can't hold as much, so the vapour condenses into cloud and rain.
questions.takeaway: Warm air holds more vapour; cooling forces the excess to condense.

questions.stem: Why do deserts tend to form where air descends in the atmospheric cells?
options: Sinking air warms and can hold more moisture but has no source of it, so it dries
Sinking air is humid and less dense, so it rises again before any rain can form
Sinking air carries dust that soaks up the rainfall before it can reach the ground
Sinking air cools and drops its moisture as rain before it ever reaches the ground
rationales: Correct. As air descends it warms and can hold more moisture, but with no moisture source it becomes drier. Rising air near the equator gives rain forests; sinking air gives deserts.
Descending air in these zones is dry, not humid.
The notes explain deserts through warming, drying air, not dust.
Sinking air warms by compression; it does not cool and rain.
questions.takeaway: Rising air → cooling → rain (rain forests); sinking air → warming → drying (deserts).

questions.stem: Which sequence describes a Hadley cell?
options: Cold air rises at the poles, flows towards the equator, sinks, then returns poleward
Warm air sinks at the equator, flows poleward at the surface, then rises at the poles
Air rises and sinks in the same place, so no surface flow occurs near the equator
Warm air rises at the equator, flows poleward, sinks, then returns along the surface
rationales: Cold polar air sinks; it does not rise.
Warm equatorial air rises, it does not sink.
The cell includes surface flow back towards the equator.
Correct. Direct sunlight warms the equator, warm air rises and is replaced by surface air; the air carried away eventually sinks and returns towards the equator, forming a cycle.
questions.takeaway: Hadley cell: rise at the equator, flow poleward aloft, sink, return at the surface.

questions.stem: Which atmospheric cells are thermally direct, and why does the remaining cell exist?
options: Ferrel and Polar are thermally direct; the Hadley cell exists because of them
All three are thermally direct, each driven by its own rising warm air
Hadley and Polar are thermally direct; the Ferrel cell exists because of them
Only the Ferrel cell is thermally direct; the other two are driven by it
rationales: The Hadley cell is driven directly by equatorial heating.
The Ferrel cell is not thermally direct; it is driven by its neighbours.
Correct. Hadley and Polar cells are driven directly by rising warm air and sinking cold air. The Ferrel cell exists because of the cells on either side.
This reverses the roles of the cells.
questions.takeaway: Hadley and Polar cells are thermally direct; the Ferrel cell is driven by them.

questions.stem: Why does Earth have three circulation cells in each hemisphere rather than a single one?
options: Each cell is anchored to a continent, so three continents give three cells
Earth is too big for one simple cycle, and Coriolis destabilises it
Mountain ranges block a single cell and cut it into three separate loops
The tilt splits heating into three fixed bands that never shift at all
rationales: Cells are global bands of circulation, not tied to continents.
Correct. Earth is too big to have one single simple cycle, and the Coriolis force also destabilises things, giving three adjacent cells.
Mountains do not split the circulation into three cells.
The cells' strength and extent do shift with the seasons.
questions.takeaway: Earth's size and the Coriolis force break circulation into Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells.

questions.stem: Where two neighbouring atmospheric cells meet, how do they move air?
options: In the same direction, so both sink or both rise there
Only sideways, so no air rises or sinks at that boundary
In random directions, depending on the day's weather
In opposite directions, so air at the boundary stalls
rationales: Correct. Where adjacent cells meet they move air in the same direction: if air sinks at one end of a cell, it also sinks at the neighbouring end of the next cell.
Boundaries between cells are where air rises or sinks.
The pattern is systematic, not random.
The cells move air the same way at their shared boundary, not against each other.
questions.takeaway: Adjacent cells move air in the same direction where they meet.

questions.stem: In the Southern Hemisphere, air flows from subtropical high pressure towards the equator. From which direction do these trade winds blow?
options: From the northeast, as the air is deflected to the left
From the southeast, as the air is deflected to the left
From the southwest, as the air is deflected to the right
From due south, since the Coriolis effect is absent there
rationales: Northeast trades are the Northern Hemisphere's, where air flows south.
Correct. Air moving north towards the equator is deflected to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, so it arrives from the southeast: the southeast trade winds.
Deflection is to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, not the Southern.
The Coriolis effect acts in both hemispheres; it is only near zero at the equator.
questions.takeaway: Southern Hemisphere: deflection to the left, giving southeast trade winds.

questions.stem: Seen from space, winds flow straight between the equator and the poles. Why do they appear to blow east or west to someone on the ground?
options: Air is pulled along by the Moon, which drags it around the Earth
The Sun heats the eastern side of the planet first each morning
Mountains steer every wind into east–west channels near the surface
The Earth spins beneath the moving air, shifting its apparent path
rationales: The notes do not explain wind deflection through the Moon.
Uneven heating drives winds, but the east–west turning comes from rotation.
Mountains affect local winds, but the global pattern comes from Earth's rotation.
Correct. Earth is spinning under the winds, so to an observer on the surface they appear to blow more east or west. This is the Coriolis effect.
questions.takeaway: The Coriolis effect: Earth rotates beneath moving air, turning its apparent path.

questions.stem: In which direction does the Coriolis effect turn the surface winds in the Hadley and Ferrel cells?
options: Westward in both cells, as Earth spins in only one direction
Eastward in the Hadley cells and westward in the Ferrel cells
Westward in the Hadley cells and eastward in the Ferrel cells
Eastward in both cells, as winds always follow Earth's spin
rationales: Surface flow in the two cells runs in opposite north–south directions, so deflection gives opposite east–west directions.
This swaps the two cells.
Correct. Earth's rotation under the winds directs them to the west in the Hadley cells (the trade winds) and to the east in the Ferrel cells (the westerlies).
Opposite north–south flows in the two cells give opposite east–west winds.
questions.takeaway: Hadley cells → easterly trade winds; Ferrel cells → westerlies.

questions.stem: What creates the jet streams?
options: Temperature and height contrasts where cells meet, plus the Coriolis effect
Trade winds converging at the equator and rising up into the upper atmosphere
Daytime sea breezes, which build up speed as they cross the open ocean
Air sinking over deserts, which speeds up sharply as it reaches the ground
rationales: Correct. Where the Polar, Ferrel and Hadley cells converge, differences in their height and temperature create turbulence; combined with the Coriolis effect, this sends narrow high-altitude streams of air from west to east.
Equatorial convergence forms the ITCZ, not the jet streams.
Sea breezes are local, daily surface winds.
Jet streams are high in the atmosphere, not formed by air sinking to the ground.
questions.takeaway: Jet streams form at cell boundaries from temperature and height contrasts plus Coriolis.

questions.stem: What are the main drivers of circulation at the ocean surface?
options: Tides raised by the Moon's gravitational pull
Heat rising from volcanoes on the ocean floor
Rivers pouring fresh water into the oceans
Prevailing winds shaped by the Coriolis force
rationales: Tides move water up and down at coasts but are not the main driver of ocean circulation.
Seafloor volcanoes are not the driver the notes describe.
River inflow is not the main driver of ocean circulation.
Correct. The prevailing winds, under the influence of the Coriolis force, are the main drivers of oceanic circulation.
questions.takeaway: Ocean surface currents are driven mainly by Coriolis-shaped prevailing winds.

questions.stem: On a sunny afternoon at the coast, which way does the breeze blow, and why?
options: From land to sea, as the sea cools faster and draws air out
From sea to land, as the land heats faster and its air rises
From sea to land, as the sea heats faster and its air rises
From land to sea, as the land heats faster and its air sinks
rationales: At night the land breeze blows out to sea, but on a sunny afternoon the flow is onshore.
Correct. By day the land is much warmer than the sea, so air rises over the land and is replaced by a sea breeze.
By day the land, not the sea, is warmer.
Warmer air rises rather than sinks.
questions.takeaway: Day: sea breeze (land warmer); night: land breeze (sea warmer).

questions.stem: Why does the summer monsoon bring very heavy rain to the slopes facing it on a high mountain range?
options: The mountains block the trade winds, so storms stall and rain out over the ocean
The ocean heats faster than the land, so dry continental air sinks onto the slopes
Land heats faster than ocean, drawing moist air inland to be forced upward
Cold air flows out of the continent, carrying moisture up the mountain slopes
rationales: The rain falls on the mountain slopes as the air is lifted, not out over the ocean.
In summer the land heats faster than the ocean, not the other way round.
Correct. In summer the land heats faster than the ocean, helping draw moist ocean air inland. Mountains force it upward, where it cools and condenses into heavy rain.
Outflowing continental air describes the dry winter monsoon.
questions.takeaway: Summer monsoon: land heats faster, moist air flows inland and is lifted to give rain.

questions.stem: What is a monsoon?
options: A seasonal prevailing wind lasting months, bringing distinct wet and dry seasons
A belt of weak winds and frequent thunderstorms lying along the equator
A daily cycle of sea breezes and land breezes along a stretch of coastline
A single intense tropical storm that forms during the warmest month of each year
rationales: Correct. A monsoon is a seasonal prevailing wind lasting several months, bringing distinct dry and wet seasons.
That describes the ITCZ (the doldrums).
Sea and land breezes are daily and local; monsoons are seasonal.
A monsoon is a seasonal wind pattern, not a single storm.
questions.takeaway: Monsoon = seasonal prevailing wind with distinct wet and dry seasons.

questions.stem: Which description fits the Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone (ITCZ)?
options: A subtropical high-pressure band where air sinks, bringing clear and very dry weather
An equatorial low where trade winds converge, with weak winds and storms
A belt of strong surface winds that blow steadily from the west towards the east
A polar band where cold air spreads out and meets the warmer westerly winds
rationales: Sinking air and clear skies describe the subtropical highs, not the ITCZ.
Correct. Trade winds converge to form the ITCZ, an equatorial low-pressure region with weak surface winds and frequent thunderstorms, known to sailors as the doldrums.
Winds in the ITCZ are weak at the surface.
The ITCZ is equatorial, not polar.
questions.takeaway: ITCZ: equatorial low where trade winds converge; weak winds, frequent thunderstorms.

questions.stem: Under normal Walker circulation conditions in the Pacific, which statement is true?
options: Trade winds pile warm water in the east, so the thermocline is deep east and shallow west
Cold water upwells mainly in the western Pacific, right beneath the warm pool
Trade winds pile warm water west, so the thermocline is deep west and shallow east
Air sinks over the warm western Pacific and rises over the cooler eastern Pacific
rationales: This reverses the normal pattern.
Upwelling of cold water happens in the east, near South America.
Correct. Westward trade winds pile warm water in the west, deepening the thermocline there; near South America it is shallow and cold water upwells.
Air rises over the warm west and sinks over the cool east.
questions.takeaway: Normal: warm pool and deep thermocline in the west; shallow thermocline and upwelling in the east.

questions.stem: The trade winds across the tropical Pacific weaken markedly. What follows in the eastern Pacific?
options: Sea surface temperatures fall there, as the warm pool retreats towards Asia
Cold water upwells more strongly, raising biological productivity offshore
The warm pool shifts west, the thermocline shallows and upwelling strengthens
The warm pool shifts east, the thermocline deepens and upwelling weakens
rationales: The warm pool moves east, so eastern Pacific waters warm.
Upwelling weakens during El Niño, lowering productivity.
This describes stronger trade winds, as in La Niña.
Correct. These are El Niño conditions: weaker trade winds, the warm pool migrating eastward, a deeper eastern thermocline, downwelling and lower productivity.
questions.takeaway: El Niño: weak trades → warm pool shifts east → deeper eastern thermocline, less upwelling.

questions.stem: In some years the fisheries off the west coast of South America collapse. How is this linked to El Niño?
options: Heavier rain over the ocean dilutes the seawater the fish rely on
Stronger trade winds drive the fish westward towards the warm pool
Weaker upwelling brings up fewer nutrients, lowering productivity
Stronger upwelling brings cold water that kills the fish near the surface
rationales: The notes link the collapse to reduced upwelling, not dilution.
Trade winds weaken during El Niño.
Correct. During El Niño the eastern thermocline deepens and downwelling replaces upwelling, lowering biological productivity, so fishing suffers.
Upwelling weakens, rather than strengthens, during El Niño.
questions.takeaway: El Niño cuts nutrient-rich upwelling, so productivity and fisheries suffer.

questions.stem: Which description fits La Niña conditions?
options: Stronger trade winds push more warm water west, increasing eastern upwelling
Weaker trade winds let the warm pool spread east, suppressing upwelling there
The trade winds reverse direction, so warm water flows towards South America
The trade winds stop entirely, so the Pacific's surface temperature evens out
rationales: Correct. La Niña has stronger trade winds, more warm water pushed westward and increased upwelling.
This describes El Niño.
La Niña strengthens the normal trade winds rather than reversing them.
La Niña strengthens the normal contrast across the Pacific.
questions.takeaway: La Niña: stronger trades, more warm water west, more upwelling east.

questions.stem: During a negative Indian Ocean Dipole, what conditions are expected?
options: Warmer waters in both east and west, with heavier rain across the basin
Cooler waters in both east and west, with drought across the whole basin
A cooler east near Java and Sumatra with less rain; a warmer, wetter west
A warmer east near Java and Sumatra with more rain; a cooler, drier west
rationales: A dipole means an east–west contrast, not uniform warming.
A dipole means an east–west contrast, not uniform cooling.
This describes the positive phase.
Correct. In the negative phase the eastern Indian Ocean is warmer than normal, raising rain and flood risk, while the west is cooler, with less rain and higher drought risk.
questions.takeaway: Negative IOD: warm, wet east (Java/Sumatra); cool, dry west. Positive IOD reverses it.

questions.stem: An El Niño and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole occur at the same time. What is the likely outcome for Indonesia?
options: Neither affects Indonesia, since both develop in distant oceans
Both favour drier conditions there, so drought risk is compounded
Both favour wetter conditions there, so flood risk is compounded
They cancel each other out, as one brings rain and the other drought
rationales: Both directly affect Southeast Asian rainfall.
Correct. El Niño brings drought to places such as Indonesia, and a positive IOD makes the eastern Indian Ocean near Java and Sumatra cooler and drier. Together they point to extreme dry conditions.
Both phases reduce rainfall around Indonesia.
Both phases push towards drier conditions there, so they reinforce rather than cancel.
questions.takeaway: El Niño plus positive IOD can combine into extreme drought in Indonesia.

questions.stem: How can a warmer ocean thousands of kilometres away change the rainfall in Singapore?
options: It cannot, because weather depends only on conditions in the local area
Ocean temperatures alter the atmosphere's circulation, shifting rain
The warm water raises sea level, which floods Singapore and causes rain
Warm water flows directly to Singapore and evaporates over the island
rationales: Distant ocean conditions clearly affect local weather through ocean-atmosphere coupling.
Correct. Ocean and atmosphere interact: changes in sea temperature alter atmospheric circulation, which shifts winds and rainfall far away. ENSO and the IOD are examples.
Rainfall changes come from shifts in circulation, not from sea-level flooding.
The effect works through the atmosphere, not water moving directly to Singapore.
questions.takeaway: Distant ocean temperatures affect local weather through ocean-atmosphere interaction.

questions.stem: A storm crosses from the northeast Pacific into the northwest Pacific without changing in strength. What happens to how it is named?
options: It becomes a cyclone, since only cyclones can cross between basins
It keeps the same name type, since names depend only on wind speed
It changes from a typhoon to a hurricane, since its winds have grown
It is renamed from hurricane to typhoon, though it is the same storm
rationales: Cyclone is the name used elsewhere, not a special category for storms crossing basins.
The names depend on region, not wind speed.
The storm moves from the hurricane region into the typhoon region, not the reverse, and strength is not the basis for the name.
Correct. Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are the same kind of storm; the name depends on the region. Northeast Pacific storms are hurricanes and northwest Pacific storms are typhoons.
questions.takeaway: Hurricane, typhoon and cyclone are one type of storm named by region.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a hurricane, a typhoon and a cyclone?
options: Only where they form; they are the same kind of storm
Their direction of spin, set by the hemisphere they form in
Their wind speed, with typhoons the strongest of the three
Their size, with cyclones being smaller than hurricanes
rationales: Correct. They are the same phenomenon: typhoons in the northwest Pacific, hurricanes in the Caribbean, western Atlantic and northeast Pacific, and cyclones elsewhere.
Spin direction depends on hemisphere, but the names follow region.
Wind speed is used for categories such as the Saffir–Simpson scale, not for these names.
Size is not what separates the names.
questions.takeaway: The three names refer to the same storm in different regions.

questions.stem: A region has very warm ocean water and an initial disturbance, but strong vertical wind shear. Why is a cyclone unlikely to develop?
options: Shear cools the ocean surface so that it can no longer supply energy
Shear cancels the Coriolis force, so the storm has nothing to make it spin
Shear tilts the storm and disrupts the vertical organisation it needs
Shear raises surface pressure, so air can no longer flow into the centre
rationales: Shear acts on the storm's structure, not on sea temperature.
Shear does not cancel the Coriolis force.
Correct. Weak shear keeps the circulation vertically aligned. Strong shear tilts the storm and disrupts its organisation.
The notes describe shear tilting and disorganising the storm, not changing surface pressure.
questions.takeaway: Strong vertical wind shear tilts and disorganises developing cyclones.

questions.stem: Why do cyclones need warm ocean water to form?
options: It supplies the heat and moisture that power the storm
It creates wind shear, which keeps the storm vertically aligned
It lowers the Coriolis force so the storm can start spinning
It cools the air high above, increasing the storm's buoyancy
rationales: Correct. Warm water, generally above about 26°C to a depth of at least 50 m, provides the energy, through heat and moisture, that drives the storm.
Weak shear is needed, and it does not come from warm water.
Warm water does not affect the Coriolis force, which depends on latitude.
Cool air at height is a separate ingredient; warm water supplies energy from below.
questions.takeaway: Warm ocean water is the cyclone's energy source.

questions.stem: The ocean at the equator is warm, yet cyclones almost never form right at the equator. Why?
options: The water at the equator is too warm, so it all evaporates before storms form
Wind shear is always strongest at the equator, tearing storms apart
The Coriolis force is near zero there, so nothing makes a storm spin
The trade winds diverge at the equator, pulling every disturbance apart
rationales: Warm water helps cyclones; it does not prevent them.
The missing ingredient at the equator is spin, not wind shear.
Correct. At the equator the Coriolis force is basically zero, so there is no spinning force to set up and sustain a cyclone. Cyclones rarely form at or cross the equator.
Trade winds converge at the equator (the ITCZ); they do not diverge.
questions.takeaway: No Coriolis force at the equator, so no cyclones form there.

questions.stem: Two coasts lie at the same tropical latitude. One has a warm ocean current offshore; the other has a cold one. Where are cyclones less likely to develop?
options: Off the cold-current coast, as cold water weakens the Coriolis force
Off the warm-current coast, as warm water raises the wind shear there
Equally off both, since latitude alone decides where cyclones form
Off the cold-current coast, as cool water supplies too little energy
rationales: Cold water reduces the energy supply; the Coriolis force depends on latitude, not temperature.
Warm water supports cyclones; it does not create shear.
Latitude matters, but sea temperature also controls development.
Correct. Cold currents inhibit cyclone development because the sea is not warm enough to supply the energy needed.
questions.takeaway: Cold ocean currents inhibit cyclones by cutting off their energy supply.

questions.stem: Which set describes a favourable atmospheric profile for cyclone formation?
options: Cool, dry low air, weak vertical wind shear and cool air at height
Warm, moist low air, weak vertical wind shear and cool air at height
Warm, moist low air, strong vertical wind shear and warm air at height
Dry low air, strong vertical wind shear and warm air at height
rationales: Cool, dry low air gives too little latent heat to fuel the storm.
Correct. Warm, moist air releases latent heat as it condenses, weak shear keeps the storm aligned, and cool air at height maximises buoyancy.
Strong shear disrupts the storm, and warm air aloft reduces buoyancy.
Each of these works against a cyclone.
questions.takeaway: Favourable profile: warm moist air below, weak shear, cool air aloft.

questions.stem: Why does cool air high in the atmosphere help a cyclone grow?
options: It increases the density contrast, so warm surface air rushes upward
It adds wind shear, which helps keep the storm's circulation lined up
It sinks to the sea surface and cools it, slowing evaporation and growth
It acts as a lid on rising air, trapping heat near the sea to fuel the storm
rationales: Correct. Cool air at height increases the density contrast and maximises buoyancy, forcing warm surface air upward in vigorous convective updrafts.
The storm needs weak shear; cool air aloft is a separate ingredient.
Cool air aloft helps the storm by boosting buoyancy, not by cooling the sea.
Cool air aloft encourages rising, not trapping.
questions.takeaway: Cool air aloft boosts buoyancy, powering strong updrafts.

questions.stem: Which sequence shows how a cyclone develops from an initial disturbance?
options: Tropical storm, tropical disturbance, tropical depression, cyclone
Tropical disturbance, tropical depression, tropical storm, cyclone
Tropical disturbance, tropical storm, cyclone, tropical depression
Tropical depression, tropical disturbance, cyclone, tropical storm
rationales: The disturbance comes before the storm stages.
Correct. A disturbance of thunderstorms becomes a depression once a surface circulation forms, then a tropical storm, then a cyclone with an eye as winds strengthen.
The depression stage comes before the tropical storm, not at the end.
The disturbance comes first, and a tropical storm precedes the cyclone.
questions.takeaway: Disturbance → depression → tropical storm → cyclone.

questions.stem: In the Northern Hemisphere, air flowing in towards a low-pressure centre is deflected to the right. Seen from above, which way does the storm rotate?
options: Clockwise, as inflowing air is turned to the right of its path
Either way, depending on the shape of the initial disturbance
Counter-clockwise, as inflowing air is turned to its right
Clockwise, as the storm simply follows the direction of Earth's spin
rationales: Rightward deflection of inflowing air produces counter-clockwise rotation, not clockwise.
The hemisphere fixes the direction through the Coriolis effect.
Correct. Air heading inward is deflected right, so it circles the low counter-clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. The Southern Hemisphere is the reverse.
The rotation comes from deflection of inflowing air, and in the north it is counter-clockwise.
questions.takeaway: Northern Hemisphere cyclones turn counter-clockwise; Southern Hemisphere ones turn clockwise.

questions.stem: How does the eye of a cyclone form?
options: The fastest winds blow at the very centre, scattering the cloud outwards
Cold air pours into the centre from above, freezing the cloud into falling ice
Air rises fastest at the centre, carrying all of the cloud up and out of the storm
Air descends into the centre where rotation is weakest, warms and clears the cloud
rationales: Winds in the eye itself are light and variable.
The descending air warms; it does not freeze the cloud.
Air sinks, not rises, in the eye.
Correct. Air descends into the storm centre where rotation is weakest; it warms, evaporating the cloud and forming the eye.
questions.takeaway: The eye forms where sinking air warms and evaporates cloud.

questions.stem: In a mature cyclone, where are winds usually strongest, and where are they lightest?
options: Strongest at the eye's edge; light and variable within the eye
Strongest in the eye itself; lightest just at the eye's edge
Strongest at the storm's outer edge; light everywhere inside it
Strongest at the outer edge, and again strongest inside the eye
rationales: Correct. Winds are relatively weak near the outer edge and fastest at the edge of the eye, while in the eye itself they may be light and variable.
The eye is calm; the fastest winds are around it.
Winds increase towards the eye; the outer edge is relatively calm.
The eye is calm, and the outer edge has relatively weak winds.
questions.takeaway: Fastest winds ring the eye; the eye itself is calm.

questions.stem: Why does very low central pressure in a cyclone contribute to storm surge?
options: Lower air pressure cools the sea, so the water expands and rises
Lower air pressure slows the winds, so water piles up offshore
Lower pressure lets the sea surface bulge up beneath the storm
Lower air pressure pulls rain inland, adding to river flooding
rationales: Pressure does not cool the sea, and cooling would shrink water, not expand it.
Low pressure is associated with stronger winds, not weaker ones.
Correct. Low pressure allows the ocean surface to rise. Together with onshore winds piling up water and shallowing seafloor, this builds the surge.
Rain flooding is a separate hazard from the surge itself.
questions.takeaway: Low pressure raises the sea surface, one of the drivers of storm surge.

questions.stem: Compared with a cyclone in more temperate latitudes, how fast does one near the equator usually move forward?
options: At the same speed, since forward motion is set by the eye's size
Faster, since warmer water pushes the storm along more quickly
Faster, since the Coriolis force is strongest close to the equator
More slowly, as the air systems around it there move slowly
rationales: The notes link forward speed to surrounding air systems, not eye size.
Warm water fuels intensity, not forward speed.
The Coriolis force is weakest near the equator, not strongest.
Correct. Forward speed is generally under 40 km/h; cyclones move faster in temperate climates, where other air systems move faster, and slower nearer the equator.
questions.takeaway: Cyclones drift slowly near the equator and speed up in temperate latitudes.

questions.stem: Which combination of processes produces a cyclone's storm surge?
options: Heavy rain over land, high river discharge, and a high tide arriving at the same time
Onshore winds piling up water, low pressure raising the sea, and shallowing seafloor
Uplift of the seafloor during the storm, displacing water just as a tsunami does
Waves from far away combining with an ordinary high tide on a calm day
rationales: Rain, rivers and tides together describe compound flooding, not the surge itself.
Correct. Storm surge comes from water piled up by onshore winds, the sea surface raised by low pressure, and shallowing water that increases height.
The seafloor does not move in a storm; that is how earthquakes make tsunamis.
Storm surge comes from the storm's winds and pressure, not distant waves on a calm day.
questions.takeaway: Storm surge = onshore winds + low pressure + shallowing seafloor.

questions.stem: Besides flooding low-lying land directly, why is a storm surge so damaging?
options: It lowers the water level, exposing the seafloor to the storm's winds
It cools the coast, making buildings and levees brittle enough to break
It reduces wave height, so the water floods the land without warning
It raises the water level so that high waves can travel further inland
rationales: A surge raises the water level, not lowers it.
Surge damage comes from water and waves, not cooling.
Surge increases the reach of waves rather than reducing them.
Correct. Storm surges flood low-lying terrain and also provide a base for high waves to move further inland.
questions.takeaway: Storm surge gives waves a raised base to reach further inland.

questions.stem: What causes the large majority of cyclone-related deaths?
options: Wind-blown flying debris
Drowning in floodwater
Triggered landslides
Collapse of buildings
rationales: Wind-blown debris is one of the other, smaller causes.
Correct. Drownings account for about 90% of cyclone-related fatalities.
Landslides are one of the other, smaller causes.
Building damage is one of the other, smaller causes.
questions.takeaway: Water, not wind, is the main killer in cyclones.

questions.stem: After a cyclone, which process most likely caused the greatest loss of property?
options: Water inundation from surge and flooding
Strong winds tearing roofs off buildings
Wind-borne missiles striking structures
Lightning strikes setting buildings alight
rationales: Correct. Water inundation results in the greatest loss of property.
Strong winds damage property, but inundation causes the greatest losses.
Wind-borne missiles are damaging, but inundation causes more loss.
Lightning is not listed among the main cyclone property impacts.
questions.takeaway: Inundation causes the greatest cyclone property losses.

questions.stem: After a cyclone, poorer informal communities rebuild in exactly the same exposed places. What does this mean for future risk?
options: Risk is unchanged, since cyclone risk depends only on the storm's wind speed
Risk falls, since rebuilding always uses stronger materials than before
Exposure and vulnerability remain, so the next cyclone can repeat the losses
Risk falls, since the same place is unlikely to be struck by a cyclone again
rationales: Risk also depends on exposure and vulnerability, not just the hazard.
Rebuilding does not guarantee stronger construction, especially in informal settlements.
Correct. Poorer informal communities are often the most vulnerable, and rebuilding in the same place keeps them exposed.
Being hit once does not lower the chance of being hit again.
questions.takeaway: Rebuilding in place without reducing vulnerability keeps risk high.

questions.stem: In recent US records, how has the main water-related cause of direct cyclone deaths shifted?
options: Storm surge kills more than ever, as coastal populations keep on growing
Wind-blown debris is now the main killer, as buildings have grown taller
Rain flooding now kills more than storm surge, as surge warnings improved
Deaths now come mainly from lightning, as storms have become stronger
rationales: Surge deaths fell as warnings and surge maps improved.
Water, not wind, causes most direct deaths.
Correct. Storm surge warnings got much better, and rainfall flooding, which reaches inland after landfall, became the main direct killer.
Lightning is not the main cause of cyclone deaths.
