questions.takeaway: With better surge warnings, inland rain flooding became the main direct cyclone killer in the US.

questions.stem: Why can deaths linked to a cyclone keep rising for weeks after the storm has passed?
options: Lightning from leftover storms causes most of the deaths after landfall
The eye passes back over the area days later, bringing the winds back again
Storm surge keeps rising for weeks after the storm has crossed the coast
Lifelines such as power, water and clinics fail, so disease spreads
rationales: The notes link later deaths to disrupted lifelines and disease, not lightning.
Cyclones move on; the eye does not return days later.
Surge is a short-lived event at landfall.
Correct. Lifelines fail: power and water outages stop treatments, closed roads and clinics delay care, and floodwater spreads infection, hitting poorer communities hardest.
questions.takeaway: Cyclone deaths continue after landfall as lifelines fail.

questions.stem: Why can a cyclone's path be monitored and forecast days ahead, unlike an earthquake?
options: Cyclones are huge and move slowly, so satellites and ships can track them
Cyclones only form near coasts, where dense networks of instruments exist
Cyclones send out P waves ahead of them, giving instruments early warning
Cyclones always follow the same tracks, so their paths are known in advance
rationales: Correct. Because cyclones move relatively slowly (compared with seismic waves) and are so large, satellites and ship-borne platforms can monitor their path.
Cyclones form over open ocean and are tracked by satellite.
P waves are seismic waves from earthquakes.
Tracks vary from storm to storm; they have to be monitored.
questions.takeaway: Large, slow cyclones can be tracked; earthquakes give only seconds of warning.

questions.stem: How do mangroves, dune systems and coral reefs help protect coastal communities from cyclones?
options: They cool the sea so cyclones always weaken before landfall
They absorb surge, break waves and reduce wave momentum
They raise the land so that surge can never reach any town
They lower wind speeds by adding friction high in the storm
rationales: They do not change sea temperature enough to weaken storms.
Correct. Mangroves, dunes and reefs absorb storm surges, break waves and reduce wave momentum.
They reduce surge and waves but have limits; they do not make towns immune.
Their effect is on water at the coast, not winds high in the storm.
questions.takeaway: Natural barriers absorb surge and wave energy, within limits.

questions.stem: A city relies on levees and flood walls for protection against cyclone surge. What warning does the notes give about such protection?
options: Protections increase wind damage to the buildings that lie behind them
Protections only fail during weak storms, never during intense ones
Protections always hold, so the land behind them needs no evacuation
Protections have limits and can fail, flooding the areas behind them
rationales: The concern is flood failure, not extra wind damage.
Intense storms are the ones most likely to exceed a protection's limit.
No protection is guaranteed, so evacuation planning is still needed.
Correct. Not all options provide protection: flood protections sometimes fail and flood the areas behind them, and most have a limit.
questions.takeaway: Flood defences have limits; failure can flood the areas they protect.

questions.stem: A cyclone makes landfall. Why does it usually begin to weaken?
options: The Coriolis force switches off over land, so the storm stops spinning
Land is colder than the eye, so the eye freezes over and then collapses
It loses its warm-water fuel, and friction over land slows its winds
Mountains add wind shear, though this has no effect on the storm's energy
rationales: The Coriolis force depends on latitude, not on land or sea.
The eye does not freeze; the storm loses its energy supply.
Correct. At landfall the fuel supply is cut, with no more evaporation from warm water, and friction over land slows the winds.
Shear does weaken storms; the main point is the lost fuel supply and friction.
questions.takeaway: Landfall cuts off the warm-water fuel supply and adds friction.

questions.stem: An AI forecasting model improved when growing storms and decaying storms were trained separately. Why did splitting help?
options: Each stage runs on different physics, so separate models fit them better
Decaying storms follow no physics at all, so they need no model
Growing storms move faster, so they need far more satellite images
Splitting doubles the amount of training data, which is all that matters
rationales: Correct. Growth is driven by the formation ingredients, while decay comes from cutting the fuel supply, shear and land friction. Different physics suits separate models.
Decay has clear physics: landfall, cooler water, shear and friction.
The split was by life stage and its physics, not storm speed.
Splitting divides the data rather than doubling it; the gain came from matching each stage's physics.
questions.takeaway: Cyclone growth and decay are driven by different physics.

questions.stem: What information do cyclone warning systems provide?
options: Alerts based on the first seismic waves, like earthquake warnings
Location, intensity and movement, forecast up to several days ahead
Only the wind speed at landfall, issued once the storm has arrived
The exact time and place a cyclone will form, weeks before it does
rationales: Cyclone warnings come from tracking the storm, not seismic waves.
Correct. Warning systems give a cyclone's location, intensity and movement up to five days ahead, updated more often as it nears.
Warnings are issued well before landfall, not only once the storm arrives.
Warnings track storms once they exist; they do not predict formation weeks ahead.
questions.takeaway: Cyclone warnings give location, intensity and movement days ahead.

questions.stem: In which stage of a thunderstorm do downdrafts dominate and cut off the supply of warm, moist air?
options: The dissipating stage, as cool air spreads out at the ground
The building stage, as warm, moist air rises and condenses
The earliest stage, before any cloud has started to form
The mature stage, as the anvil forms near the tropopause
rationales: Correct. In the dissipating stage, downdrafts dominate; cool air spreads out at the ground and cuts off the warm, moist air, so the updraft weakens.
The building stage is dominated by updrafts.
Before cloud forms there are no storm downdrafts.
The mature stage has downdrafts alongside updrafts, but they do not yet dominate.
questions.takeaway: Thunderstorm stages: building (updrafts) → mature (both) → dissipating (downdrafts).

questions.stem: Why are thunderstorms especially common at latitudes near the equator?
options: Strong, steady winds there carry storms in from higher latitudes
Cold, dry air sinks steadily, compressing and heating up the ground
Warm, moist, unstable air rises rapidly, condenses and releases heat
The Coriolis force is strongest there, spinning the air into storms
rationales: Near-equatorial thunderstorms form locally rather than being carried in.
Sinking, dry air suppresses storms.
Correct. Thunderstorms form as unstable, warm and moist air rapidly rises into colder air and condenses, releasing heat and driving the updraft.
The Coriolis force is weakest near the equator.
questions.takeaway: Thunderstorms grow from warm, moist, unstable air rising and releasing latent heat.

questions.stem: Lightning in Singapore peaks during the inter-monsoon months rather than during the monsoons. What explains this?
options: Cooler air in those months makes the atmosphere very stable
Strong monsoon winds then carry storms in from the open sea
The ITCZ moves far away then, leaving only lightning behind
Light, variable winds then favour local, intense thunderstorms
rationales: A stable atmosphere suppresses thunderstorms.
Inter-monsoon months lack strong prevailing winds.
Lightning comes with thunderstorms; it does not occur on its own.
Correct. The inter-monsoon months have predominantly light and variable winds, which favour localised, intense thunderstorms.
questions.takeaway: Light, variable inter-monsoon winds favour local thunderstorms and lightning.

questions.stem: How does a thunderstorm build up the charge that lightning later releases?
options: Friction between the cloud and the ground builds charge in the soil
Colliding ice particles transfer charge, and updrafts separate it
Falling rain carries positive charge down, leaving the cloud negative
Sunlight charges the cloud top, while the sea charges its base
rationales: The charge builds inside the cloud, not through friction with the ground.
Correct. Collisions between ice particles transfer charge, and updrafts and falling particles separate it, leaving the cloud top mainly positive and the base mainly negative.
The cloud ends up with a positive top and negative base, not wholly negative.
Charge separation happens within the cloud, not from sunlight or the sea.
questions.takeaway: Ice collisions transfer charge; updrafts separate it top from bottom.

questions.stem: Why are tall objects beneath a thunderstorm more likely to be struck by lightning?
options: Tall objects reach right up into the cloud, where all lightning is generated
Tall objects are usually made of metal, and lightning only ever strikes metal
The negative cloud base draws positive charge up, gathering on tall objects
The positive cloud base draws negative charge upward through the tallest objects
rationales: Tall objects do not reach into the cloud; they concentrate the attracted charge.
Lightning does not strike only metal.
Correct. The negative cloud base attracts positive charge to the ground beneath it, especially around tall objects; when the field is strong enough, lightning discharges.
The cloud base is mainly negative, not positive.
questions.takeaway: Positive ground charge gathers on tall objects beneath the negative cloud base.

questions.stem: What causes thunder?
options: Clouds collide in the sky, and the impact creates a loud boom of sound
Lightning heats air so fast it expands, then contracts, making sound
Charge leaving the ground pulls the air apart in a sudden sonic boom
Raindrops fall through the lightning channel and burst into steam
rationales: Clouds do not produce thunder by colliding.
Correct. Lightning rapidly heats the air, which expands rapidly, then cools and contracts, generating sound waves.
Thunder comes from rapid heating and expansion of air along the flash.
Thunder comes from the heated air itself, not raindrops.
questions.takeaway: Thunder is the sound of air rapidly heated and expanded by lightning.

questions.stem: You hear thunder 6 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. Sound travels about 340 m every second. Roughly how far away was the lightning?
options: About 6 km away
About 340 m away
About 20 km away
About 2 km away
rationales: This treats each second as a kilometre; sound covers only about a third of a kilometre per second.
That is the distance sound travels in one second, not six.
This is far too large for a six-second delay.
Correct. Light arrives almost instantly, so the delay is the sound's travel time: 6 × 340 m ≈ 2 km.
questions.takeaway: Distance to lightning ≈ seconds of delay × 340 m.

questions.stem: Why does thunder rumble on rather than arriving as a single crack?
options: Sound from the near part of the flash arrives before sound from the far part
The air keeps heating for minutes after the flash, which stretches out the sound
Lightning strikes many times a second along one path, and each strike is heard
The sound bounces back and forth between the base and the top of the cloud
rationales: Correct. We hear thunder from the closest part of the flash first and the farthest part last, which causes the rumble.
The heating is extremely brief; the rumble comes from different travel distances.
The rumble is explained by distance along the flash, not repeated strikes.
Echoes within the cloud are not the explanation given.
questions.takeaway: Thunder rumbles because sound arrives from near and far parts of the flash at different times.

questions.stem: Why are downbursts from strong thunderstorms dangerous to aircraft close to the ground?
options: They cause sudden wind shear, so planes can lose lift from under their wings
They pull aircraft upward into the cloud, where lightning then strikes them
They carry volcanic ash downward, damaging jet engines near the runway
They drive hail into the engines, which then fail during take-off or landing
rationales: Correct. Downbursts are areas of rapidly descending air that cause wind shear, a sudden change in wind speed or direction, which can make planes lose lift.
Downbursts push air down, not up.
Downbursts are not linked to volcanic ash.
The danger described is wind shear, not hail in the engines.
questions.takeaway: Downbursts create wind shear that can rob aircraft of lift near the ground.

questions.stem: What allows hailstones to grow large inside a thunderstorm?
options: Warm air near the ground melts and refreezes them into big stones
Weak updrafts let them fall slowly, picking up snow as they go
Strong updrafts carry them up and down, adding layers of ice
Lightning fuses small ice pellets together into a single stone
rationales: Hail grows high in the cold atmosphere, not near the warm ground.
Large hail needs strong updrafts to keep it aloft.
Correct. Strong updrafts carry droplets high where they freeze; repeated up-and-down movement adds layers of ice until the hailstones are too heavy for the updraft.
Lightning does not build hailstones.
questions.takeaway: Hail grows as strong updrafts cycle it through cold air, adding ice layers.

questions.stem: Where does a delta form?
options: Where a river splits around a mountain and drops all of its heaviest rocks
Where a river enters slower water that cannot carry away its sediment
Where a river speeds up through a narrow gorge and erodes its bed
Where seawater flows inland and leaves sediment on the river bed
rationales: Deltas form at a river's mouth, where it meets slower water, not around mountains.
Correct. A delta is a low-lying landform built by sediment a river deposits as it enters slower-moving or stagnant water that cannot carry the sediment away.
Speeding up and eroding is the opposite of what builds a delta.
The sediment comes from the river, not the sea.
questions.takeaway: Deltas form where a river's sediment is dropped into slower water.

questions.stem: As a delta builds out into the sea and the river's course becomes longer, what must happen to the river bed further upstream?
options: It stays fixed, as only the mouth of the river is ever affected
It falls, as a longer river cuts down deeper into its bed
It moves sideways only, as rivers never change in height
It rises, as the river's grade adjusts to its longer course
rationales: The whole profile adjusts, not just the mouth.
The bed rises rather than cuts down as the profile lengthens.
River beds do change in height as the profile adjusts.
Correct. As the river profile lengthens, the river bed at each point along its course has to rise so its grade adjusts to the increasing length.
questions.takeaway: A delta growing seaward lengthens the river, so its bed must rise upstream.

questions.stem: Why does a delta's seaward growth matter to people living along the lower reaches of its river?
options: The river bed and water level rise relative to the land beside it
The river runs dry as the growing delta soaks up all of its water
The river speeds up, cutting a deep canyon through their land
The coastline retreats inland, moving the sea closer towards them
rationales: Correct. As the delta grows seaward, the river bed must rise, so the river sits higher relative to the surrounding land, with important consequences for flooding.
Delta growth does not dry the river up.
The river's grade adjusts by raising its bed, not by cutting a canyon.
Seaward growth moves the coastline outward, not inland.
questions.takeaway: Delta growth raises the river relative to the lower floodplain, raising flood risk.

questions.stem: A delta has many distributary channels, some now only weakly connected to the main river. What does this suggest?
options: Every channel carries equal flow, since deltas share water evenly
The main flow has shifted over time, leaving older channels behind
The sea carved the channels by flowing up the river at high tide
The older channels were dug by people to drain water off the delta
rationales: The notes show some channels are much more active than others.
Correct. The most active distributaries are those still connected to the main river; others were more active when the main river fed them, showing the flow has shifted (avulsion).
The channels are distributaries carrying river water and sediment out to sea.
These are natural distributaries, not drainage channels.
questions.takeaway: Deltas shift their main channels over time, leaving older distributaries behind.

questions.stem: On a natural delta, floods and shifting channels spread fresh sediment widely. What happens once people confine the river with levees?
options: Compaction stops, as the levees take weight off the land behind
Sediment builds up behind the levees, raising the land steadily
Sediment no longer reaches the land, which sinks as it compacts
Nothing changes, as sediment has no effect on the land's height
rationales: Compaction of sand, mud and organic material continues regardless.
Levees keep sediment in the channel, not on the land behind them.
Correct. Levees stop floods and avulsions delivering sediment, so the land keeps compacting with nothing to replace it and sinks.
Sediment supply is what keeps a delta's surface up.
questions.takeaway: Levees starve deltas of sediment, so compacting land sinks.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT included when a storm surge is measured?
options: The rise in water above the normal tide
Water piled up by strong onshore winds
Sea level lifted by low air pressure
The height of the waves breaking on top
rationales: This is exactly what storm surge measures.
Wind-driven piling up of water contributes to the surge.
Low pressure raising the sea contributes to the surge.
Correct. Storm surge is measured as the rise in water level above the normal tidal level and does not include waves.
questions.takeaway: Storm surge = rise above normal tide, excluding waves.

questions.stem: Which situation is the clearest example of compound flooding?
options: A tsunami reaching a coast with no rain, wind or river flooding at the same time
A river rising slowly over several weeks after snow melts far upstream
A single heavy downpour flooding city streets on an otherwise calm day
Storm tide, heavy rain and high river flow combining to flood a coastal city
rationales: A tsunami alone is a single driver.
This is one slow driver, not a combination.
A single driver acting alone is not compound flooding.
Correct. Compound flooding combines several drivers, such as storm tides and waves, precipitation, river discharge and sea-level rise.
questions.takeaway: Compound flooding: several drivers (surge, rain, river flow, sea level) combine.

questions.stem: A moderate high tide and moderate rainfall occur together. Neither is extreme on its own, but together they cause severe flooding. How should this be classified?
options: As a compound event, since non-extreme events can combine into an extreme impact
As a single event, since only the larger of the two drivers is counted as a cause
Not as a compound event, since compound events must involve two separate extremes
As a cascading event, since one of the two hazards must have triggered the other
rationales: Correct. One definition of compound events includes combinations of events that are not themselves extremes but lead to an extreme event or impact when combined.
Compound events count the combination of drivers, not just one.
Compound events can involve non-extreme contributors.
A cascade requires one event to trigger another; here they simply coincide.
questions.takeaway: Compound events can arise from non-extreme drivers combining.

questions.stem: As relative sea level rises, a moderate storm that once caused no flooding now floods a coastal town. Why?
options: Higher sea level slows the waves, so the water lingers longer on the land
The same surge now starts from a higher base, so it reaches higher ground
Higher sea level makes storms stronger, so the surges are now much larger
The storm must be stronger than before, as surges never rise on their own
rationales: The problem is the higher starting level, not slower waves.
Correct. Sea level is the baseline on which storm surges occur. A surge of the same size, starting from a higher base, reaches higher and further inland.
Sea-level rise raises the baseline; it does not by itself make storms stronger.
The storm can be the same; the baseline is what changed.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise raises the baseline, so ordinary surges flood more.

questions.stem: Which set lists the mechanisms of coastal flooding given in the notes?
options: Tsunamis, soil liquefaction, and glacial isostatic adjustment of land
Heavy precipitation, uplift of the coast, and the cooling of seawater
Storm surges and tsunamis, heavy precipitation, and relative sea-level rise
Storm surges, river avulsions, and the slow thermal contraction of the seawater
rationales: Liquefaction and glacial isostatic adjustment are not listed as flooding mechanisms.
Coastal uplift and cooling seawater reduce flood risk rather than causing it.
Correct. Coastal flooding mechanisms include storm surges and tsunamis, heavy precipitation and relative sea-level rise.
Thermal contraction would lower sea level, not cause flooding.
questions.takeaway: Coastal flooding: surges and tsunamis, heavy rain, relative sea-level rise.

questions.stem: Which pair are the two main global causes of sea-level rise?
options: Coastal uplift in earthquakes, and growth of large deltas
Seawater shrinking as it cools, and growing sea ice
More rain over the oceans, and rivers carrying more water
Seawater expanding as it warms, and melting land ice
rationales: These are local land movements, not global causes of rising seas.
Cooling and growing ice would lower sea level.
Rain and rivers move water around the water cycle rather than adding to the ocean long term.
Correct. Warming makes seawater expand (thermal expansion), and melting glaciers and ice sheets add water to the ocean.
questions.takeaway: Global sea-level rise: thermal expansion plus melting land ice.

questions.stem: Long after the last ice age ended, land that lay under thick ice sheets is still slowly rising. Why?
options: It is rebounding now that the heavy weight of the ice has been removed
Sea level is falling everywhere, which only makes the land look higher
Thermal expansion of the rock beneath is lifting the land as it warms
New ice is forming deep under the land and pushing the surface upward
rationales: Correct. Post-glacial rebound is the rise of land after the huge weight of ice sheets was removed. Glacial isostatic adjustment is still ongoing.
Global sea level is rising, not falling; the land itself is moving up.
The rise comes from rebound after the ice load was removed, not thermal expansion of rock.
The land is rebounding from ice that has gone, not being pushed up by new ice.
questions.takeaway: Glacial isostatic adjustment: land still rebounding after ice-age ice sheets melted.

questions.stem: Two coastal towns experience the same global sea-level rise, but one sees a much faster relative rise. What best explains the difference?
options: Relative rise depends only on how far each town is from the poles
The ocean rises more at some coasts because the water is denser
The faster town's land is subsiding, adding to the global rise
The faster town's land is being uplifted, adding to the rise
rationales: Distance from the poles is not the controlling factor here.
The notes explain local differences through land motion, not density.
Correct. Relative sea level combines ocean rise with vertical land motion. A sinking coast adds to the global rise, so it experiences faster relative rise.
Uplift would reduce relative sea-level rise, not increase it.
questions.takeaway: Relative sea-level rise = ocean rise + land subsidence (or minus uplift).

questions.stem: Why do the notes say tectonics matters for sea-level projections in Southeast Asia?
options: Earthquakes heat the ocean water, adding directly to thermal expansion
Earthquake cycles raise or lower coasts, changing relative sea level
Tectonic motion is already fully included in every sea-level projection
Tectonic plates change the volume of the ocean basins every single year
rationales: Earthquakes do not measurably heat the ocean.
Correct. In much of Southeast Asia tectonics is a local issue: earthquakes uplift or lower coasts, changing relative sea level, yet it is rarely incorporated into projections.
The notes say tectonics is rarely incorporated into projections.
Tectonics affects local land height, not ocean basin volume year to year.
questions.takeaway: Tectonic land motion changes relative sea level but is rarely in projections.

questions.stem: After a great subduction earthquake, a weak mantle layer beneath the region slowly flows back toward the trench. How can this affect a city far from the trench?
options: Its land can slowly sink for decades, raising its relative sea level
Its sea level falls, since the trench slowly draws the nearby water away
Its land rises sharply, removing its coastal flood risk for good
It is unaffected, since only land right beside the trench moves
rationales: Correct. Slow mantle motion after a great earthquake can raise some land near the trench but make land farther away sink over time, raising relative sea level there.
Sinking land raises relative sea level; the trench does not draw water away.
The distant land sinks rather than rises.
The effect reaches far beyond the trench.
questions.takeaway: Post-earthquake mantle flow can make distant coasts subside for decades.

questions.stem: During the last glacial maximum, global sea level was far lower than today. Why?
options: The land everywhere was pushed up, moving the shoreline far out to sea
The oceans were warmer, so the seawater took up less room in the basins
Rivers stopped flowing, so the oceans slowly evaporated away into space
Large amounts of water were locked up in expanded ice sheets on land
rationales: Ice actually pushed land down (isostatic depression); sea level fell because water was locked in ice.
It was colder, not warmer; colder water also takes up less space, but ice storage was the main cause.
Water was stored as ice, not lost to space.
Correct. Global ice cover rose sharply during the last glacial maximum, locking water on land, so sea level dropped by over 100 m.
questions.takeaway: Ice ages lower sea level by locking water up in land ice.

questions.stem: Why do accurate sea-level projections for a coast need global, regional and local processes together?
options: Regional processes cancel out over time, so only global ones matter
Local land motion can add to or offset global ocean rise at any coast
Global processes are too small to matter compared with the local tides
Each process acts in only one place, so all of them must be listed
rationales: Regional and local processes can dominate locally, as subsidence shows.
Correct. Sea level at a coast reflects global ocean rise plus regional and local processes such as subsidence, tectonics and glacial isostatic adjustment, so all are needed.
Global rise is a major driver everywhere.
Processes overlap and combine at every coast; they are not each confined to one place.
questions.takeaway: Projections must combine global ocean rise with regional and local land motion.

questions.stem: Why have the older parts of a large delta sunk over time?
options: Wind erosion slowly removing the top layers of the sediment
Uplift of the river mouth, which slowly tilts the old delta downward
Compaction of sand and mud and the oxidation of organic material
Melting of ice layers buried deep beneath the delta sediment
rationales: Wind erosion is not the explanation given.
The notes do not describe tilting by uplift at the mouth.
Correct. Older parts of the delta have sunk mainly because sand and mud compact and organic material in the sediments oxidises.
Deltas do not contain buried ice layers.
questions.takeaway: Delta sediments sink through compaction and oxidation of organic matter.

questions.stem: Parts of a large coastal city are sinking far faster than global sea level is rising. What is the most likely main cause?
options: Earthquake uplift reversing after many quiet years have passed
Glacial isostatic adjustment from a former ice sheet nearby
Groundwater extraction, compacting the soft clays beneath the city
Thermal expansion of all the seawater lying directly under the city
rationales: This is not the cause the notes identify for rapid urban sinking.
Tropical delta cities were not under ice sheets.
Correct. Groundwater-related subsidence can make cities sink by many centimetres a year, much faster than global sea-level rise, especially on compactable clay.
Thermal expansion raises sea level; it does not sink the land.
questions.takeaway: Groundwater pumping can make cities sink faster than the sea rises.

questions.stem: Which combination makes a low-lying delta city both sink and flood more?
options: Strong uplift from earthquakes, and sediment delivered by river floods
Hard bedrock underneath, only a few buildings, and falling regional sea level
Cool ocean water, lightweight buildings, and frequent river avulsions
Groundwater pumping, heavy buildings on compactable clay, and rising seas
rationales: Uplift and sediment supply raise land rather than sink it.
These would all reduce sinking and flooding.
None of these is identified as driving urban sinking.
Correct. Uncontrolled groundwater extraction, the sheer weight of urban build-up on compactable clay, more intense rain and sea-level rise together drive sinking and flooding.
questions.takeaway: Urban sinking: groundwater pumping + building weight on soft clay, worsened by sea-level rise.

questions.stem: A delta city lies below sea level, protected by levees. What happens if a storm surge overtops or breaches the levees?
options: Little flooding occurs, as levees slow the water to a trickle
Water floods in and stays, as the land lies lower than the sea
Water drains away quickly, as the land slopes down to the sea
Only the levees are damaged, as surge cannot travel further in
rationales: A breach lets water pour through, not trickle.
Correct. Land below sea level fills like a bowl once levees are overtopped or breached, and water cannot drain back out naturally.
Land below sea level cannot drain back to the sea by gravity.
Once levees fail, surge water floods the low land behind them.
questions.takeaway: Below-sea-level cities behind levees flood catastrophically if the levees fail.

questions.stem: Floods that spread sand across a delta are a natural process. Why do they turn into disasters in delta cities?
options: People settle the floodplain and cut off the sediment that kept land up
Natural floods are disasters anyway, whether or not anyone lives there
Floods carry far more sand than before, burying deltas faster than ever
Sand laid down by floods weakens the levees until they finally collapse
rationales: Correct. Flooding and sediment deposition are natural; human activities removed the sediment supply and placed people in harm's way, turning a natural process into a disaster.
A hazard only becomes a disaster when it affects an exposed, vulnerable society.
The process has not become more extreme; the setting has changed.
The notes do not blame flood sand for weakening levees.
questions.takeaway: Natural delta flooding becomes disaster when people settle there and cut off sediment.

questions.stem: Which are the three response strategies to sea-level rise named in the notes?
options: Retreat, accommodate and defend
Defend, insure and wait it out
Accommodate, relocate and drain
Retreat, evacuate and rebuild
rationales: Correct. The three strategies are planned retreat, accommodate (adapt) and defend or protect with soft or hard engineering.
Insurance and waiting are not among the three strategies.
Draining the sea is not a strategy in the notes.
Evacuation and rebuilding are not the named strategies.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise responses: retreat, accommodate, defend.

questions.stem: A coastal town raises its houses on stilts and lets seasonal flood water pass beneath them. Which strategy is this?
options: Defend, using hard engineering to keep the sea out of the town entirely
Planned retreat, moving people away from the coastline to safer ground
Accommodate, letting natural effects occur while limiting the impacts
Defend, using soft engineering such as restoring the coastal wetlands
rationales: Stilts let water in rather than keeping it out.
People stay in place, so this is not retreat.
Correct. Accommodation lets natural system effects occur while minimising human impacts.
No wetlands are being restored; the town is adapting its buildings.
questions.takeaway: Accommodate = live with the water while minimising its impact.

questions.stem: A city compares building a seawall with restoring mangroves and wetlands along its coast. How do these fit the response strategies?
options: The seawall is planned retreat, while the mangroves count as accommodation
Neither is a way to defend, since defending means abandoning the coastline
The mangroves are planned retreat, as they push the shoreline further inland
Both defend: one by hard engineering, the other by soft, nature-based means
rationales: A seawall defends; it does not retreat.
Abandoning the coastline is retreat, not defence.
Mangroves protect the shoreline rather than retreat from it.
Correct. Defend or protect can use hard engineering, such as seawalls and barriers, or soft engineering, such as nature-based solutions like mangroves and wetlands.
questions.takeaway: Defend can be hard (seawalls) or soft (nature-based solutions).

questions.stem: Why might planned retreat be chosen despite its heavy social costs?
options: It lets the coast keep its levees, since nobody needs to maintain them
It minimises losses and can be the most cost-effective long-term response
It is always the cheapest option in the very first year of any project
It stops sea level from rising, since people no longer live along the coast
rationales: Retreat is not about keeping levees.
Correct. Planned retreat minimises losses and maximises the cost-effectiveness of the response.
Retreat is justified by long-term outcomes, not first-year cost.
Retreat changes exposure; it does not affect sea level itself.
questions.takeaway: Planned retreat minimises long-term losses and can be the most cost-effective option.

questions.stem: A huge movable barrier that closes across an estuary when a storm approaches is an example of what?
options: Defence by hard engineering against storm surge
A nature-based solution built from living systems
Accommodation by letting surge water pass freely
Planned retreat away from a vulnerable estuary
rationales: Correct. A storm surge barrier is hard engineering used to defend against surge.
It is an engineered structure, not a living system.
The barrier blocks surge rather than letting it pass.
The barrier keeps people in place and protects them; it is not retreat.
questions.takeaway: Storm surge barriers are hard-engineering defences.

questions.stem: On short timescales, what mainly controls Earth's surface temperature?
options: How close the Earth sits to the Moon at different times
How quickly the tectonic plates move across the mantle
How much sunlight is reflected and how much is absorbed
How much heat escapes the core through volcanic eruptions
rationales: The Moon's distance is not a control on surface temperature in the notes.
Plate motion is far too slow to control surface temperature on short timescales.
Correct. On shorter timescales, Earth's surface temperature is influenced by how much sunlight is reflected and absorbed.
Heat from the core is not the main control on surface temperature.
questions.takeaway: Surface temperature depends on how much sunlight is reflected versus absorbed.

questions.stem: Compared with a clear night, why is a cloudy night usually warmer at the ground?
options: Clouds stop cold air from sinking down from higher altitudes
Clouds release heat they stored from the Sun during the day
Clouds reflect leftover sunlight back down onto the ground at night
Clouds trap the infrared radiation given off by the ground
rationales: The effect comes from trapped radiation, not blocked cold air.
The notes show clouds trapping outgoing infrared radiation, not releasing stored solar heat.
There is no sunlight at night to reflect.
Correct. At night the ground gives off infrared radiation; cloud cover traps it, so a cloudy night stays warmer than a clear one.
questions.takeaway: Clouds trap outgoing infrared at night, keeping the ground warmer.

questions.stem: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Gases in the atmosphere reflect incoming sunlight, cooling the surface
Gases in the atmosphere trap heat given off by the surface, warming it
Gases form aerosols that block sunlight, just as volcanic SO₂ does
Gases thin out the atmosphere, letting much more sunlight reach the ground
rationales: Reflecting sunlight would cool; greenhouse gases warm by trapping outgoing heat.
Correct. Greenhouse gases such as CO₂ trap heat radiated from Earth's surface, warming the lower atmosphere and surface.
Aerosols from SO₂ cool the climate, the opposite of the greenhouse effect.
Greenhouse gases do not thin the atmosphere.
questions.takeaway: Greenhouse effect: atmospheric gases trap heat radiated from the surface.

questions.stem: How do volcanic SO₂ and CO₂ from burning fossil fuels differ in their effect on climate?
options: SO₂ traps heat and warms for a long time; CO₂ forms aerosols that cool briefly
Both trap heat, but SO₂ does so far more strongly and for much longer than CO₂
SO₂ forms aerosols that cool briefly; CO₂ traps heat and warms for a long time
Both form aerosols that reflect sunlight, cooling the climate for several years
rationales: The two roles are swapped.
SO₂'s main climate effect is cooling through aerosols.
Correct. Volcanic SO₂ forms sulphate aerosols that reflect sunlight and temporarily cool the climate, while CO₂ is a greenhouse gas that warms over the long term.
CO₂ warms; it does not form reflecting aerosols.
questions.takeaway: SO₂ aerosols cool briefly; CO₂ warms long-term.

questions.stem: Why is the link between CO₂, water vapour and warming described as a positive feedback loop?
options: Warming raises evaporation and vapour, which adds still more warming
Water vapour forms clouds that always reflect sunlight and cool Earth
Warming lowers evaporation and vapour, which then cools the climate
Water vapour helps crops grow, which is good for the environment
rationales: Correct. Greenhouse warming increases evaporation, and warmer air holds more water; more water vapour increases greenhouse warming, so the cycle reinforces itself.
The loop described is about vapour trapping heat, which amplifies warming.
Warmer air holds more vapour, not less.
Positive here means self-reinforcing, not beneficial.
questions.takeaway: Positive feedback = self-reinforcing: warming → more vapour → more warming.

questions.stem: If human CO₂ emissions stopped today, why would global temperature not fall significantly for a very long time?
options: The oceans would suddenly absorb all the CO₂ and then freeze over
CO₂ already taken up by the oceans would slowly be released back
Volcanoes would immediately replace all of the CO₂ humans stopped
Plants would stop taking up CO₂ once all human emissions had ended
rationales: The oceans release, rather than suddenly absorb, stored CO₂.
Correct. CO₂ added to the oceans would slowly release back to the atmosphere, preventing a significant temperature drop for at least 1,000 years.
Volcanic output does not suddenly rise to replace human emissions.
Plants do not stop taking up CO₂ when emissions stop.
questions.takeaway: Ocean-stored CO₂ returning to the air keeps temperatures high long after emissions stop.

questions.stem: Why is the amount of CO₂ in the atmosphere rising?
options: The seasonal cycle of CO₂ has grown stronger each year
Volcanic activity has risen sharply over recent decades
Plants and oceans have released all of their stored CO₂
Human emissions exceed what plants and oceans take up
rationales: The seasonal cycle sits on top of the long-term rise; it does not cause it.
The notes attribute the rise to human emissions, not volcanoes.
Plants and oceans are still taking up CO₂; they just cannot keep pace.
Correct. CO₂ from human activities is greater than what plants and oceans can take up, so the excess accumulates.
questions.takeaway: CO₂ accumulates because human emissions outpace natural uptake.

questions.stem: A small rise in average temperature shifts the whole temperature distribution towards warmer values. What happens to extremely hot days?
options: They fall, since a warmer average narrows the spread of temperatures
They rise sharply, as once-rare hot days become far more frequent
They rise by the same small amount as the average temperature does
They stay just as rare, since only the middle of the curve moves
rationales: The distribution has actually broadened, not narrowed.
Correct. Shifting the whole bell curve makes temperatures that were once rare much more frequent, so extreme heat increases disproportionately.
A small shift in the average causes a much larger change at the hot tail.
The whole distribution shifts, including the tails.
questions.takeaway: A small average shift makes once-rare extreme heat much more common.

questions.stem: As the planet has warmed, the distribution of temperatures has also become broader. What is the most likely reason?
options: Cold extremes have become more common everywhere
Every region is warming at exactly the same rate
Weather stations have been removed in recent years
Different regions are warming at different rates
rationales: The distribution shifts warmer; cold extremes are not becoming more common everywhere.
Identical warming everywhere would shift the curve without broadening it.
The notes do not attribute the broadening to station changes.
Correct. The broadening is most likely due to differential regional warming.
questions.takeaway: Uneven regional warming broadens the temperature distribution.

questions.stem: Why can a heatwave persist for days under a stationary high-pressure system?
options: Sinking air warms by compression and suppresses cloud, so heat builds up
Low pressure draws warm ocean air inland, where it sits for several days
Strong winds keep blowing hot air in from deserts, refreshing the heat
Rising air cools and forms cloud, which then traps the heat underneath
rationales: Correct. Persistent high pressure makes air sink and warm through compression, suppressing cloud and rain. Clear skies allow strong solar heating, and the pattern lets heat build over days.
Heatwaves are linked to high pressure, not low.
Heatwaves under high pressure have weak, not strong, winds.
High pressure brings sinking, not rising, air.
questions.takeaway: Heatwaves: high pressure → sinking, warming air → clear skies → heat builds.

questions.stem: Air sinking under a heatwave's high-pressure system warms up. Which earlier concept explains this warming?
options: Latent heat, released by condensation inside the sinking air
The Coriolis effect, turning sinking air towards the equator
Adiabatic warming, as sinking air is compressed and heats
Thermal expansion, as the air expands while it sinks and warms
rationales: Sinking air suppresses cloud, so there is little condensation.
Coriolis changes wind direction, not temperature.
Correct. Falling air compresses and warms adiabatically, the reverse of rising air expanding and cooling.
Sinking air is compressed, not expanded.
questions.takeaway: Sinking air warms by compression (adiabatic warming).

questions.stem: Recent sea-level rise is broken down into two main modelled causes. What are they?
options: More rain falling over the oceans, and more water in rivers
Seafloor uplift under the oceans, and coastal land sinking
Seawater shrinking as the ocean cools, and growing glaciers
Seawater expanding as the ocean warms, and melting land ice
rationales: These move water around rather than raising the long-term ocean level.
These are local land motions, not the two global modelled causes.
Cooling and growing glaciers would lower sea level.
Correct. The two main causes are sea water expansion from ocean warming and melting land-based glaciers and ice sheets.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise = thermal expansion + melting land ice.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a consequence of sea-level rise listed in the notes?
options: Coastal populations being forced to move
Low levees overtopped during flood events
Stronger earthquakes along faults nearby
Salt water getting into freshwater aquifers
rationales: Displacement of coastal populations is a listed consequence.
Low levees being overtopped during floods is a listed consequence.
Correct. Sea-level rise is not listed as making earthquakes stronger.
Salt water contaminating freshwater aquifers is a listed consequence.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise: coastal flooding, salty aquifers, overtopped levees, displacement.

questions.stem: For a large, low-lying delta nation, why is simply raising levees everywhere not a practical answer to sea-level rise?
options: Raising levees across such vast areas would cost far too much money
Levees cannot be built on deltas, as the sediment there is too hard
Levees would make floods less frequent, which the land cannot cope with
Sea-level rise will stop by itself before levees would be needed
rationales: Correct. Raising levees across a vast delta would be cost-prohibitive, especially where floods already affect a large share of the land.
Delta sediment is soft, not too hard, and levees are built on deltas.
The barrier is cost, not reduced flooding.
Sea level reacts slowly and will keep rising for a long time.
questions.takeaway: For vast deltas, raising levees everywhere is cost-prohibitive.

questions.stem: As sea level rises, wells in a coastal town begin to taste salty. What has most likely happened?
options: Rain has become saltier as the ocean evaporates more quickly
Seawater has pushed into the fresh aquifer under the town
The town's pipes have corroded, releasing salt into its water
Sea spray from storms has slowly collected inside the wells
rationales: Evaporation leaves salt behind in the ocean, so rain is fresh.
Correct. Rising seas let salt water contaminate freshwater aquifers.
Corrosion is not the consequence of sea-level rise described.
Spray does not explain groundwater turning salty.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise drives salt water into coastal freshwater aquifers.

questions.stem: Why will sea level keep rising for centuries even if global warming were to stop?
options: Sea level reacts instantly, so the rise will stop the moment warming stops
Sea level is set by plate tectonics, which no climate action can affect
Sea level reacts slowly to warming, so the rise continues long afterwards
Sea level depends only on rainfall, which will keep rising regardless
rationales: The response is slow, not instant.
Tectonics affects local relative sea level, but the global rise is driven by warming.
Correct. Sea level reacts very slowly to global warming, so once started, the rise continues for thousands of years.
Rainfall is not the driver; thermal expansion and ice melt are.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise lags warming and continues for a very long time.

questions.stem: The Keeling Curve of atmospheric CO₂ shows two patterns. What are they?
options: A falling long-term trend with no seasonal change at all
A seasonal cycle on top of a rising long-term trend
A steady level broken only by sudden volcanic jumps
A daily cycle that has stayed flat over the decades
rationales: The long-term trend is rising, and there is a clear seasonal cycle.
Correct. The Keeling Curve, the longest record of directly measured CO₂, shows a seasonal cycle superimposed on a long-term rise.
The record shows a steady rise with a seasonal cycle, not volcanic jumps.
The plotted cycle is seasonal and the trend is rising.
questions.takeaway: Keeling Curve: seasonal cycle on a rising long-term trend.

questions.stem: How do ice cores show that today's atmospheric CO₂ level is unusual?
options: Ice records past CO₂, which long stayed in a far lower range
Ice records past eruptions, which released more CO₂ than today
Ice records past sea levels, which were always higher than today
Ice records only temperature, so past CO₂ has to be guessed
rationales: Correct. Ice cores trace past climate: for hundreds of thousands of years CO₂ stayed in a lower range, far below today's level.
Past CO₂ never reached today's level, so eruptions did not release more.
Ice cores are used here to trace past CO₂, not sea level.
Ice cores record past CO₂ directly, not just temperature.
questions.takeaway: Ice cores show CO₂ today is far outside its range of the past several hundred thousand years.

questions.stem: Over one decade, global temperature rises very little even though emissions keep growing. How do the notes explain this?
options: Warming has stopped, so emissions no longer affect global temperature
Rising emissions cool the climate over periods of about a decade
The records must be wrong, since warming always rises perfectly steadily
Natural variability can temporarily dampen or boost the warming trend
rationales: A short pause does not mean warming has ended or that emissions no longer matter.
Emissions warm the climate; natural variability explains the pause.
Year-to-year natural variability means warming is not perfectly steady.
Correct. Over short timescales, typically a decade, natural variability can temporarily dampen or accentuate global warming trends.
questions.takeaway: Natural variability can mask or boost the warming trend over a decade.

questions.stem: According to the IPCC summary in the notes, what must happen for global temperature to stabilise?
options: CO₂ emissions need to stop growing
CO₂ emissions need to fall by half
CO₂ in the air needs to double once
CO₂ emissions need to reach net zero
rationales: Emissions that stay flat still add CO₂, so warming continues.
Halving emissions still adds CO₂ each year.
Doubling CO₂ would cause more warming, not stabilise it.
Correct. For temperature to stabilise, CO₂ emissions need to reach net zero.
questions.takeaway: Temperature stabilises only when CO₂ emissions reach net zero.

questions.stem: How does peat form?
options: Organic matter builds up faster than it decays in waterlogged ground
Organic matter decays quickly in dry, airy soil, leaving carbon behind
Seawater floods coastal forests, turning the wood into salt deposits
Volcanic ash buries forests, which are then compressed into hard rock
rationales: Correct. Peat forms when organic matter accumulates faster than it decomposes, because waterlogged conditions lack oxygen.
Dry, airy soil speeds decay, which prevents peat from building up.
Peat is accumulated organic matter, not salt.
Peat forms from waterlogged organic matter, not from buried forests turned to rock.
questions.takeaway: Peat: organic matter accumulating faster than it decays in waterlogged, low-oxygen ground.

questions.stem: Why are fires in drained peatlands so hard to put out?
options: They spread only through treetops, out of reach of fire crews
They burn down towards the water table and smoulder for months
They burn so hot that water turns to steam before reaching them
They restart each day from lightning, which is common over peat
rationales: Peat fires burn in the ground, not the treetops.
Correct. In dried peat, fires can penetrate the ground to near the water table, smouldering undetected for months, even after rain or under snow, and spreading far.
The difficulty is that they burn underground, not their temperature.
Peat fires persist by smouldering underground, not by daily lightning.
questions.takeaway: Drained peat fires smoulder underground for months and are hard to extinguish.

questions.stem: A peat swamp forest is drained and cleared for plantations. What is the likely consequence for the climate?
options: Peat stops forming, but none of the carbon already stored is affected
Draining locks the carbon away more tightly, which helps cool the climate
The dried peat can burn and release its stored carbon, adding to warming
Plantations store more carbon than peat does, so emissions fall overall
rationales: Stored carbon in dried peat is exposed to burning and decomposition.
Draining exposes the carbon to oxygen and fire rather than locking it away.
Correct. Draining removes the waterlogging that keeps peat intact, so it can burn and release its carbon. Peatlands are the most carbon-dense land ecosystem.
Peatlands store far more carbon than plantations.
questions.takeaway: Draining peat turns a carbon store into a carbon source.

questions.stem: Why do peatlands matter so much in climate change, despite covering a fairly small area of land?
options: They produce most of the world's oxygen, offsetting human CO₂ emissions
They reflect more sunlight than any other ecosystem, cooling the planet
They are the most carbon-dense land ecosystem, storing vast carbon stocks
They hold little carbon but give off large amounts of SO₂ when they are wet
rationales: Their importance lies in stored carbon, not oxygen production.
Peatlands are dark and waterlogged; their importance is carbon storage.
Correct. Peatlands are the most carbon-dense of any land ecosystem, storing more carbon than much larger ecosystems.
Peatlands hold a great deal of carbon.
questions.takeaway: Peatlands are the most carbon-dense land ecosystems.

questions.stem: Which action best protects a peatland's role as a carbon store?
options: Keeping the peat waterlogged so organic matter does not decompose
Draining the peat so that it dries out and is easier to farm on
Burning the surface vegetation regularly to control its growth
Replacing the peat swamp forest with industrial plantations
rationales: Correct. Waterlogged, low-oxygen conditions are what let peat accumulate and keep its carbon.
Draining dries the peat, making it vulnerable to fire and decay.
Fires used to control vegetation can spread into dried peat and smoulder for months.
Conversion to plantations destroys peatlands.
questions.takeaway: Keep peat wet to keep its carbon locked away.

questions.stem: What links earthquakes induced by wastewater injection with landslides triggered by heavy rain?
options: Water dissolves the rock, removing material that held it in place
Water cools the rock, which shrinks and cracks along weak surfaces
Added water weight crushes rock, forming brand-new faults and slopes
Raised fluid pressure cuts friction, letting faults or slopes slip
rationales: Neither case is explained by dissolving rock in the notes.
Cooling and shrinking is not the mechanism in either case.
Injection lets existing faults slip; it does not crush rock into new faults.
Correct. Injected fluid raises underground pressure so existing faults slip; rain raises pore fluid pressure in slopes, reducing friction. The same principle drives both.
questions.takeaway: Higher fluid pressure reduces friction, triggering both induced earthquakes and landslides.

questions.stem: Storm surges and tsunamis both flood coasts. Which statement correctly contrasts them?
options: Both come from seafloor movement, but surges happen only in shallow coastal water
Surge comes from storm winds and low pressure; a tsunami from water displacement
Both come from storm winds, but tsunamis form only when the tide is at its highest
Surge comes from sudden water displacement; a tsunami from storm winds and low pressure
rationales: Storm surges are caused by the storm, not by seafloor movement.

Correct. Storm surge is water piled up by onshore winds and raised by low pressure in a storm; a tsunami comes from sudden displacement of a large volume of water, by earthquakes, landslides or eruptions.
Tsunamis are not caused by storm winds.
The causes are swapped.
questions.takeaway: Surge = storm winds + low pressure; tsunami = sudden displacement of water.

questions.stem: Why can a cyclone's landfall be forecast days ahead, while an earthquake warning gives only seconds?
options: Cyclones send out early seismic waves, while earthquakes have no waves to detect at all
Cyclones are huge and slow to move, while earthquake warnings rely on the P–S wave gap
Cyclones form near dense instrument networks, while earthquakes occur far out at sea
Cyclones always follow fixed tracks, while earthquakes strike at entirely random places
rationales: Earthquakes, not cyclones, produce seismic waves; that is what early warning uses.
Correct. Large, slow cyclones can be tracked by satellite for days. Earthquake early warning can only use the short time between fast P waves and damaging S and surface waves.
Cyclones form over open ocean and are tracked by satellite; earthquakes occur on land and at sea.
Cyclone tracks vary and must be monitored.
questions.takeaway: Warning time depends on the hazard: days for slow cyclones, seconds for earthquakes.

questions.stem: A coastal city lies inland of an oceanic trench where an oceanic plate subducts beneath a continent. Which set of geohazards should it plan for?
options: Only gentle basaltic lava flows and slow creep on nearby hillslopes
Normal-fault earthquakes and rift volcanism as the continent splits
Hotspot eruptions and earthquakes on transform faults off the coast
Megathrust earthquakes, tsunamis and explosive volcanoes in the arc
rationales: Subduction zones are far more hazardous than this; arc volcanoes are often explosive.
Normal faulting and rift volcanism belong to divergent settings.
Hotspots and transforms are not the defining hazards of a subduction margin.
Correct. Subduction zones host great thrust earthquakes that can generate tsunamis, and water released from the slab feeds arc volcanoes, which tend to erupt viscous magma explosively.
questions.takeaway: Subduction margins combine megathrust earthquakes, tsunamis and explosive arc volcanoes.

questions.stem: During a megathrust earthquake, the land along one stretch of coast subsides. How does this change its future coastal flood risk?
options: Relative sea level falls there, so tides and surges no longer reach the land
Flood risk falls, as the earthquake has released all the strain on the fault
Relative sea level rises there, so tides and surges reach further inland
Nothing changes, as only global sea level matters for coastal flooding
rationales: Subsidence raises relative sea level; uplift would lower it.
Releasing strain does not undo the subsidence that has already happened.
Correct. Coseismic subsidence lowers the land, raising relative sea level, so the same tides and surges reach further.
Local vertical land motion matters as well as global sea level.
questions.takeaway: Earthquake subsidence raises relative sea level and coastal flood risk.

questions.stem: What do lahars, debris flows and turbidity currents have in common?
options: All are fast flows of sediment and water going downslope
All are slow movements that take many years to unfold
All happen only on land, far away from rivers and seas
All are triggered only by eruptions at stratovolcanoes
rationales: Correct. A lahar is a volcanic mixture of water and rock fragments, a debris flow is a fast wet landslide, and a turbidity current is a submarine debris flow.
All three are fast-moving flows.
Turbidity currents happen under the sea.
Only lahars are linked to volcanoes, and they can also be triggered by rain.
questions.takeaway: Lahars, debris flows and turbidity currents are all fast sediment-and-water flows.

questions.stem: The same deflection caused by Earth's rotation explains which pair of observations?
options: Northeast trade winds, and Northern Hemisphere cyclones turning counter-clockwise
Seafloor magnetic stripes, and the steady drift of plates away from mid-ocean ridges
Sea breezes during the day, and the long, rumbling sound of thunder after lightning
The arrival of P waves before S waves, and the slowing of tsunamis in shallow water
rationales: Correct. The Coriolis effect deflects moving air: Northern Hemisphere trade winds blow from the northeast, and air flowing into a low spins counter-clockwise there.
Magnetic stripes come from field reversals and spreading, not Coriolis.
Sea breezes come from uneven heating and the rumble from distance along the flash.
Wave arrival order and tsunami speed depend on wave type and water depth.
questions.takeaway: The Coriolis effect shapes both prevailing winds and cyclone spin.

questions.stem: A strong El Niño brings drought to Indonesia. Which cascading hazard does this make more likely there?
options: Colder seas spawn more cyclones, which then strike the coastline
Rising groundwater liquefies deltas during the next earthquake
Heavier monsoon rain saturates hillslopes, triggering more landslides
Drier peatlands catch fire more easily, releasing carbon and haze
rationales: Cyclones need warm water, and colder seas would suppress them.
Drought lowers groundwater rather than raising it.
El Niño brings drought to Indonesia, not heavier rain.
Correct. El Niño drought dries the land; drained or dried peat burns easily and smoulders for months, releasing stored carbon. Haze is listed among weather-related hazards.
questions.takeaway: Climate variability can cascade: El Niño drought → peat fires → carbon release and haze.

questions.stem: Which monitoring technique from the notes maps ground displacement from space both after earthquakes and during volcanic inflation?
options: Seismic tomography, mapping the speed of seismic waves
Infrasound, picking up very low-frequency sound waves
InSAR, comparing radar phase between satellite passes
DART buoys, measuring pressure changes on the seafloor
rationales: Tomography images the subsurface rather than mapping surface displacement.
Infrasound detects explosions, not ground displacement.
Correct. InSAR compares radar phase from two passes to map line-of-sight ground displacement, used for coseismic slip and for volcano deformation.
DART buoys detect tsunamis, not ground deformation.
questions.takeaway: InSAR maps surface displacement for both earthquakes and volcanoes.

questions.stem: Why are cities built on young river deltas doubly exposed during strong earthquakes?
options: Their hard bedrock carries seismic waves further without the waves weakening
Their young, saturated sediments liquefy, and soft ground amplifies shaking
Their position at plate boundaries means they sit right above every rupture
Their river channels guide surface waves inland at speeds far above P waves
rationales: Deltas sit on soft sediment, not hard bedrock.
Correct. Liquefaction is most severe in young, saturated deposits in deltas and coastal areas, and soft sediments amplify shaking in strength and duration.
Deltas are not defined by plate boundaries.
Surface waves are the slowest waves, and rivers do not speed them up.
questions.takeaway: Delta sediments both liquefy and amplify earthquake shaking.

questions.stem: How does long-term sea-level rise affect the reach of a future tsunami of the same size?
options: It is unaffected, since tsunamis come from earthquakes, not the sea
It travels faster, as deeper water near the coast adds to its height
It starts from a higher baseline, so it can reach further inland
It is reduced, since deeper water absorbs more of the wave's energy
rationales: Tsunamis flood from the sea's level, so that baseline matters.
A slightly deeper coastal sea does not make the tsunami taller; the higher baseline is what matters.
Correct. Sea level is the baseline on which storm surges and tsunamis occur, so a higher sea lets the same wave reach higher and further inland.
Higher sea level raises flooding rather than absorbing the wave.
questions.takeaway: Sea-level rise raises the baseline for both tsunamis and storm surges.

questions.stem: Across earthquakes, cyclones and floods, what most consistently decides who dies when the same hazard strikes two places?
options: How far the place lies from the nearest plate boundary or from the equator
Vulnerability and protection: building quality, warnings and evacuation
Whether the hazard is a geohazard or a weather-related hazard in that place
The exact physical size of the hazard, which is always larger in poorer places
rationales: Location shapes the hazard, but deaths depend on vulnerability and protection.
Correct. Throughout the course, hazards become disasters through exposure and vulnerability: buildings kill in earthquakes, drowning dominates cyclones, and evacuation and protection save lives.
Both kinds of hazard become disasters through vulnerability.
The same hazard can produce very different outcomes; its size alone does not decide who dies.
questions.takeaway: Hazards are natural; disasters come from vulnerability and lack of protection.

questions.stem: According to the IPCC summary in the notes, how does further global warming change tropical cyclones?
options: A larger share of cyclones become intense
Fewer cyclones form, and all of them are weaker
Cyclone strength and number stay unchanged
Cyclones start to form right on the equator
rationales: Correct. The IPCC summary shows the proportion of intense tropical cyclones rising with each step of warming.
The summary points to more intense cyclones, not weaker ones.
The summary shows cyclones changing with warming.
The Coriolis force is still near zero at the equator, so this does not change.
questions.takeaway: Warming raises the share of intense tropical cyclones.

questions.stem: Rising warm, moist air feeds both thunderstorms and cyclones. Which process powers the updraft in both?
options: Lightning heating the air, which makes the whole cloud expand upward
Cold air sinking from above, which pushes warm air up beside it
Coriolis deflection, which turns horizontal winds into vertical ones
Latent heat released as water vapour condenses in rising air
rationales: Lightning is a result of the storm's charge separation, not its power source.
Downdrafts weaken thunderstorms in the dissipating stage; they do not power the updraft.
Coriolis gives cyclones spin, not their rising energy, and thunderstorms do not need it.
Correct. Condensation releases latent heat, warming the air so it keeps rising, which drives thunderstorm updrafts and cyclone convection alike.
questions.takeaway: Latent heat from condensation powers both thunderstorms and cyclones.

questions.stem: Why can a magma rich in silica and a slope saturated with water both lead to sudden, violent failure?
options: Both lose all their heat quickly, so they crack apart as they rapidly cool
Pressure builds that the material cannot release until it suddenly gives way
Both lower the driving force, so the material collapses under its own weight
Both are pulled downslope by the Coriolis force once they reach a threshold
rationales: Neither failure is explained by cooling and cracking.
Correct. Stiff, silica-rich magma traps gas until pressure fragments it explosively; water in a slope raises pore pressure and reduces friction until the slope suddenly fails.
Failure happens when driving force exceeds resistance, not when it falls.
The Coriolis force plays no part in either.
questions.takeaway: Trapped pressure, whether gas in magma or water in a slope, can end in sudden failure.

questions.stem: GNSS stations appear throughout the course. Which pairing of setting with what GNSS reveals is correct?
options: Plate boundary: strain build-up; volcano: inflation from recharge
Plate boundary: shaking intensity; volcano: the chemistry of its gases
Plate boundary: magma storage depth; volcano: tsunami travel time
Plate boundary: cyclone tracks; volcano: infrasound from its explosions
rationales: Correct. GNSS tracks slow interseismic strain and plate motion, and records ground inflation at volcanoes that suggests magma recharge.
Intensity comes from damage surveys, and gas chemistry from gas sampling.
Storage depth comes from petrology, and tsunami timing from ocean instruments.
GNSS does not track cyclones or record infrasound.
questions.takeaway: GNSS measures ground motion: plate strain and volcanic inflation.
